rows.anchor: 114.6 — Experiment 1 ... System records 'test failed.' Is this an observation? Potentially. But if it stores only status=FAILED without source, time or context, its evidentiary value is limited. Expected: Observation=Partial unless richer semantics exist. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 1: a bare status=FAILED value without source/time/context yields Observation=Partial; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 114.7 — Claim ... A claim should be distinguishable from raw document, observation, recommendation, decision. Claim: Component A violates Rule B. This claim can then be supported by Evidence.
rows.statement: States a Claim must be distinguishable from raw document/observation/recommendation/decision, illustrated by a component-violates-rule claim supportable by evidence.

rows.anchor: 114.8 — Experiment 2 ... An AI agent produces 'The implementation violates the architecture.' No claim object exists. Expected: this is an assertion produced by the agent, not necessarily a first-class KnowledgeOS claim. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 2: an AI agent's assertion without a backing claim object is merely an agent assertion, not a first-class KnowledgeOS claim; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 114.9 — Decision ... We need to determine whether the implementation distinguishes Recommendation from Decision. This is one of the most important semantic boundaries.
rows.statement: States distinguishing Recommendation from Decision as one of the most important semantic boundaries to test for.

rows.anchor: 114.10 — Experiment 3 ... A generated architecture recommendation is stored in the same table as an approved architecture decision. No type, authority or lifecycle distinguishes them. Expected: DecisionSemantics=Weak. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 3: a recommendation and an approved decision sharing one undifferentiated table with no type/authority/lifecycle distinction yields DecisionSemantics=Weak; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 114.11 — Authority ... A system may have user_id and role without implementing decision authority. We need Authority→Scope→Permission→DecisionType.
rows.statement: States Authority is harder to establish than role, requiring Authority->Scope->Permission->DecisionType beyond a bare user_id/role pair.

rows.anchor: 114.12 — Experiment 4 ... User has ROLE_ARCHITECT but the system does not restrict which decisions that user may make. Expected: role exists, authority semantics are not established. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 4: a ROLE_ARCHITECT role without decision-type restriction shows role exists but authority semantics do not; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 114.13 — Action ... we ask whether the system can reconstruct Who+What+Why+When+AgainstWhat+UnderWhichAuthority. This is particularly important for AI agents.
rows.statement: States Action testing requires reconstructing Who+What+Why+When+AgainstWhat+UnderWhichAuthority, particularly important for AI agents.

rows.anchor: 114.14 — Experiment 5 ... Session logs show 'file changed' but not agent identity, command, intent, authorization. Expected: ActionProvenance=Partial. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 5: session logs recording only 'file changed' without identity/command/intent/authorization yield ActionProvenance=Partial; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 114.15 — Provenance ... This may be the most important cross-cutting semantic concept. Provenance(X)=Source+Actor+Time+Transformation+Context. The actual implementation may support only some of these.
rows.statement: Defines Provenance(X)=Source+Actor+Time+Transformation+Context, called possibly the most important cross-cutting semantic concept.

rows.anchor: 114.16 — Experiment 6 ... Document has source_url. Expected: source attribution exists, but this does not establish complete provenance. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 6: a source_url field establishes partial source attribution, short of complete provenance; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 114.17 — Temporal validity ... We need to distinguish CreatedAt from ValidFrom. These are not the same. A decision can be created today but become effective next month.
rows.statement: States CreatedAt≠ValidFrom, illustrated by a decision created today but becoming effective next month.

rows.anchor: 114.18 — Experiment 7 ... Object contains created_at but no effective/supersession semantics. Expected: creation timestamp exists, temporal validity remains unproven. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 7: an object with only created_at and no effective/supersession fields leaves temporal validity unproven; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 114.19 — Semantic relationship test ... The concepts themselves are not enough. We need relationships. Evidence-supports->Claim. Claim-informs->Decision. Decision-authorizes->Action.
rows.statement: States concept-level evidence is insufficient; relationships (Evidence-supports->Claim, Claim-informs->Decision, Decision-authorizes->Action) must also be tested.

rows.anchor: 114.20 — Experiment 8 ... Two records exist: Decision, Evidence. No explicit relationship connects them. Expected: both concepts may exist independently, but Decision↔Evidence semantics are not established. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 8: independently existing Decision and Evidence records with no explicit relationship leave Decision<->Evidence semantics unestablished; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 114.21 — Semantic edge test ... For every important edge A-r->B we require evidence of the relationship, its direction, its meaning, its lifecycle.
rows.statement: Defines the semantic edge test requiring evidence of relationship existence, direction, meaning, and lifecycle for every important edge.

rows.anchor: 114.22 — Experiment 9 ... A decision has evidence_ids[]. Expected: strong evidence of a relationship. But we still need to know does the system enforce that those IDs actually represent supporting evidence? Result: S1/S2 not automatically S3
rows.statement: Experiment 9: a Decision's evidence_ids[] field is strong relationship evidence at S1/S2, but not automatically S3 without enforced verification that the IDs represent genuine supporting evidence.

rows.anchor: 114.23 — Relationship semantics versus foreign keys ... A foreign key says A.id→B.id. It does not necessarily say A-supports->B. The semantic meaning must be established.
rows.statement: States a foreign key (A.id->B.id) does not necessarily establish a semantic relationship (A-supports->B); semantic meaning must be independently established.

rows.anchor: 114.24 — Experiment 10 ... decision_id appears in an audit table. Expected: it does not prove that the audit record is evidence supporting the decision. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 10: a decision_id foreign key in an audit table does not prove the audit record is evidence supporting the decision; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 114.25 — Semantic lifecycle test ... Lifecycle(C). Draft→Reviewed→Approved→Effective→Superseded.
rows.statement: Defines the semantic lifecycle test Lifecycle(C), illustrated by Draft->Reviewed->Approved->Effective->Superseded.

rows.anchor: 114.26 — Experiment 11 ... Database enum contains DRAFT, APPROVED. Expected: state representation exists, but transition rules remain unknown. Result: S1
rows.statement: Experiment 11: a DRAFT/APPROVED enum shows state representation (S1) with transition rules still unknown.

rows.anchor: 114.27 — Experiment 12 ... Application code rejects Draft→Effective without approval. Expected: an actual semantic invariant is being enforced. Result: S2/S3 depending on verification
rows.statement: Experiment 12: application code rejecting an unapproved Draft->Effective transition shows an actual enforced semantic invariant, graded S2/S3 depending on verification.

rows.anchor: 114.28 — Semantic invariant test ... A semantic core is strongest when its invariants are executable. ApprovedDecision⇒AuthorityExists. Then assert decision.authority != null or an equivalent domain constraint.
rows.statement: States a semantic core is strongest with executable invariants, illustrated by ApprovedDecision⇒AuthorityExists as an executable assertion.

rows.anchor: 114.29 — Experiment 13 ... Rule exists only in an ADR. Expected: SpecifiedInvariant. Not ImplementedInvariant. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 13: a rule existing only in an ADR is SpecifiedInvariant, not ImplementedInvariant; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 114.30 — Cross-concept invariant ... The most interesting invariants span concepts. Decision→Evidence. Action→Decision/Authorization. These are more valuable than isolated field validation.
rows.statement: States cross-concept invariants (Decision->Evidence, Action->Decision/Authorization) are more valuable than isolated field validation.

rows.anchor: 114.31 — Experiment 14 ... Agent action is accepted without a corresponding authorization decision. Expected: potential semantic/governance violation. Result: OBS/VIOL
rows.statement: Experiment 14: an accepted agent action with no corresponding authorization decision is a potential semantic/governance violation, classified OBS/VIOL.

rows.anchor: 114.32 — Semantic authority chain ... Authority→Decision→Action→Observation→Evidence with Provenance connecting each step. This creates a complete organizational feedback loop.
rows.statement: Proposes the stronger target chain Authority->Decision->Action->Observation->Evidence with Provenance connecting each step, forming a complete organizational feedback loop.

rows.anchor: 114.33 — But this is not yet the implementation ... We must resist a major temptation. We cannot say 'KnowledgeOS has this architecture' yet. The correct statement is: this is the semantic-core hypothesis against which the implementation is being tested.
rows.statement: Warns against prematurely claiming the target model as actual architecture, insisting on the correct framing as a hypothesis under test.

rows.anchor: 114.34 — Semantic-core evidence matrix ... Concept x Representation/Behavior/Verification/Runtime/Authority/Relationships for the eight concepts, all cells '?'. This is now the central empirical artifact.
rows.statement: Presents the formal semantic-core evidence matrix (eight concepts x six columns, all cells '?') as the central empirical artifact.

rows.anchor: 114.35 — Evidence grades ... 0=No evidence, 1=Mentioned, 2=Represented, 3=Behavior implemented, 4=Verified, 5=Runtime proven, 6=Governed. Grade(C)∈[0,6].
rows.statement: Defines an ordinal evidence-grade scale 0 (No evidence) through 6 (Governed), Grade(C)∈[0,6].

rows.anchor: 114.36 — Experiment 15 ... Concept appears in architecture documentation only. Grade=1. Expected: not implemented. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 15: a documentation-only concept is Grade=1, not implemented; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 114.37 — Experiment 16 ... Concept has code and tests but no runtime evidence. Grade=4. Expected: verified implementation, runtime status unknown. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 16: a code-and-tests-but-no-runtime-evidence concept is Grade=4; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 114.38 — Experiment 17 ... Concept is implemented, tested and demonstrably used in production. Grade=5. If ownership and governance are also established: Grade=6. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 17: a production-demonstrated concept is Grade=5, rising to Grade=6 with established ownership/governance; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 114.39 — The semantic-core score ... SemanticCoreStrength=sum(w_i*Grade(C_i))/sum(w_i). But we should not calculate it yet. The individual evidence matters more than a synthetic score.
rows.statement: Defines but explicitly defers the SemanticCoreStrength weighted-average formula, stating individual evidence matters more than a synthetic score.

rows.anchor: 114.40 — Why not score now? ... Evidence=5 but Authority=1. A high average could conceal a critical weakness. Therefore Vector>Scalar. We retain the individual dimensions.
rows.statement: States Vector>Scalar: averaging per-dimension grades (e.g. Evidence=5, Authority=1) could conceal a critical weakness, so individual dimensions must be retained.

rows.anchor: 114.41 — Semantic completeness ... Are the essential relationships present? Evidence→Claim, Claim→Decision, Decision→Action, Action→Observation. Missing one critical edge may be more significant than several missing optional features.
rows.statement: Defines semantic completeness as essential-relationship-edge presence, stating one missing critical edge may outweigh several missing optional features.

rows.anchor: 114.42 — Experiment 18 ... All eight concepts exist. But no Decision→Authority. Expected: semantic core remains incomplete. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 18: all eight concepts present but no Decision->Authority edge leaves the semantic core incomplete; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 114.43 — Semantic core minimum ... Core_minimum. A semantic core is not defined by how many entities exist. It is defined by the minimum relationships necessary to preserve the meaning of the system.
rows.statement: Defines Core_minimum: a semantic core is defined by the minimum relationships necessary to preserve system meaning, not by entity count.

rows.anchor: 114.44 — Experiment 19 ... KnowledgeOS has documents, embeddings, search, chat history, vector retrieval. But no Authority or Decision semantics. Expected: it may be a sophisticated knowledge retrieval system, but the semantic core remains weak. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 19: a system with documents/embeddings/search/chat-history/vector-retrieval but no Authority/Decision semantics is a sophisticated retrieval system with a weak semantic core; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 114.45 — This is the decisive distinction ... Knowledge Retrieval Platform: Documents→Embeddings→Retrieval. Knowledge Operating System: Knowledge→Evidence→Reasoning→Decision→Action→Observation→UpdatedKnowledge. The second has organizational state and control semantics.
rows.statement: Draws the decisive distinction between a Knowledge Retrieval Platform (Documents->Embeddings->Retrieval) and a Knowledge Operating System (Knowledge->Evidence->Reasoning->Decision->Action->Observation->UpdatedKnowledge), the latter possessing organizational state and control semantics.

rows.anchor: 114.46 — Feedback loop ... KNOWLEDGE→EVIDENCE→REASONING→DECISION→ACTION→OBSERVATION→NEW EVIDENCE→KNOWLEDGE. This is the operating-system loop we are testing for.
rows.statement: Presents the full feedback-loop diagram Knowledge->Evidence->Reasoning->Decision->Action->Observation->NewEvidence->Knowledge, explicitly named the operating-system loop under test.

rows.anchor: 114.47 — Agent integration ... Agent→Reasoning, Agent→Recommendation, Agent→Action. But authority should remain explicit.
rows.statement: States agents participate in the loop via Reasoning/Recommendation/Action, with authority required to remain explicit.

rows.anchor: 114.48 — Experiment 20 ... Agent generates recommendation. Expected: Recommendation→Human/PolicyDecision. Not Recommendation=Decision. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 20: an agent recommendation must route to Human/PolicyDecision, never equated directly with Decision; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 114.49 — Autonomous action ... If an agent can act autonomously, the semantic model needs DelegatedAuthority. HumanAuthority→Delegates→AgentAuthority. Then AgentAction→DelegatedAuthority.
rows.statement: Defines DelegatedAuthority (HumanAuthority-delegates->AgentAuthority; AgentAction->DelegatedAuthority) as required for autonomous agent action.

rows.anchor: 114.50 — Experiment 21 ... Agent has credentials allowing production changes. No explicit delegation record exists. Expected: technical capability exists, semantic authority is not established. Result: PASS. This distinction is extremely important for AI governance.
rows.statement: Experiment 21: production-change credentials without an explicit delegation record show technical capability without semantic authority, called extremely important for AI governance; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 114.51 — Provenance of AI reasoning ... We should also distinguish ModelOutput from DecisionEvidence. An LLM's explanation can be useful, but it is not automatically authoritative evidence.
rows.statement: Distinguishes ModelOutput from DecisionEvidence, stating an LLM's explanation is not automatically authoritative evidence.

rows.anchor: 114.52 — Experiment 22 ... Agent says 'I verified the architecture.' No tool execution or evidence exists. Expected: UnverifiedAIAssertion. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 22: an agent's unverified self-report of having verified the architecture, with no tool execution, is an UnverifiedAIAssertion; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 114.53 — Tool-backed verification ... Agent→VerificationTool→DeterministicResult→Evidence. This is consistent with the deterministic assurance architecture established earlier.
rows.statement: Defines tool-backed verification Agent->VerificationTool->DeterministicResult->Evidence, consistent with the established deterministic assurance architecture.

rows.anchor: 114.54 — Experiment 23 ... Agent runs an architecture test. Test produces PASS. Evidence includes test, commit, environment, timestamp. Expected: strong verification evidence. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 23: an agent-run architecture test producing PASS with a full evidence bundle (test/commit/environment/timestamp) is strong verification evidence; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 114.55 — Semantic core and KnowledgeOS identity ... If Search, AgentHooks, Governance, Audit, VectorDB all exist but cannot be connected through a coherent semantic model, then the platform may be architecturally fragmented.
rows.statement: Defines a KnowledgeOS identity test: whether major capabilities (Search/AgentHooks/Governance/Audit/VectorDB) connect through one coherent semantic model, or the platform is architecturally fragmented.

rows.anchor: 114.56 — Experiment 24 ... Every subsystem has a different definition of 'knowledge.' Expected: SemanticFragmentation. Result: DRIFT CANDIDATE
rows.statement: Experiment 24: every subsystem defining 'knowledge' differently is SemanticFragmentation, classified DRIFT CANDIDATE.

rows.anchor: 114.57 — The strongest possible finding ... If the actual repository shows KnowledgeObject=Document+Embedding but no Evidence/Decision/Authority model, the correct conclusion is: the current implementation provides knowledge retrieval/management capabilities, but the richer KnowledgeOS semantic oper
rows.statement: States that finding KnowledgeObject=Document+Embedding without Evidence/Decision/Authority is a valuable finding (not a failure), correctly characterizing the system as a retrieval platform whose semantic operating model is not yet implemented.

rows.anchor: 114.58 — Conversely ... If the repository demonstrates Evidence, Decision, Authority, Provenance, Verification and their relationships, then we have evidence that the KnowledgeOS architecture is materially implemented.
rows.statement: States the converse positive finding: demonstrated Evidence/Decision/Authority/Provenance/Verification with relationships would be evidence of material KnowledgeOS implementation.

rows.anchor: 114.59 — Step 114 verdict ... ConceptualSemanticCore≠ProvenActualSemanticCore until the repository evidence fills the matrix. STEP 114 — SEMANTIC CORE TEST: READY FOR EMPIRICAL EXECUTION.
rows.statement: Records the Step 114 verdict ConceptualSemanticCore≠ProvenActualSemanticCore pending matrix completion, marked READY FOR EMPIRICAL EXECUTION.

rows.anchor: Step 115 — Semantic Graph Reconstruction preview ... G_actual=(V_actual,E_actual) where nodes are real concepts and edges are actual relationships (supports, implements, verifies, authorizes, produces, derivedFrom, supersedes, contradicts). Decisive experiment: can an actual KnowledgeOS decision be
rows.statement: Previews Step 115: reconstructing the actual graph G_actual=(V_actual,E_actual) over real concepts/relationships, with the decisive backward/forward decision-traceability experiment determining whether a genuine knowledge operating loop exists or which links are missing.

lexical.anchor: We now test the semantic-core hypothesis against the actual KnowledgeOS implementation. Which of these concepts are actually first-class concepts in the current system? Only evidence of actual implementation counts as implementation evidence.

formal.anchor: 114.1 — The evidence test ... T(C)=(Code,Schema,API,Tests,Runtime,Owner,Relations). S0 Terminology only, S1 Represented, S2 Behavioral, S3 Verified, S4 Operational, S5 Governed.

operational.anchor: 114.6 — Experiment 1 ... System records 'test failed.' Is this an observation? Potentially. But if it stores only status=FAILED without source, time or context, its evidentiary value is limited. Expected: Observation=Partial unless richer semantics exist. Result: PASS

notations: K_OS={x | x has an evidenced architectural role in KnowledgeOS}

sources.note: Step 110: the empirical/evidence-based system-boundary classification methodology, distinct from the earlier THEORETICAL DDD bounded-context proposals (bounded-context-map B0002, epistemic-bounded-context-map-v1 B0012) in that it classifies ACTUALLY DISCOVERED artifacts (via CORE/SUPPORTING/AGENT/EXTERNAL/LEGACY/UNKNOWN) rather than proposing a target context decomposition. Key contributions: K_OS defined by evidenced architectural role not mere interaction; LogicalBoundary!=DeploymentBoundary; three-tier K_product/K_ecosystem/K_environment containment; Projection!=Ownership; dependency-direction-independent ownership (caller/callee direction does not determine system ownership); InfrastructureDependency!=KnowledgeModel; the key finding RepositoryMembership!=SystemMembership with a BuildGraph/DeploymentGraph/RuntimeGraph three-stage operational-membership test; nine-verb relationship-semantics vocabulary (Consumes/Produces/Reads/Writes/Publishes/Subscribes/Verifies/Authorizes/Projects); BoundaryEvidence record schema; and five named invariants I_Boundary/I_AuthorityBoundary/I_RuntimeMembership/I_AgentBoundary/I_External. Resolves the Claude/Codex agent-boundary question from Steps 105/107/109 (EcosystemParticipants with AgentOperatingLayers, not core). Extends evidence-based-architecture-reconstruction-methodology (S1008); previews Step 111 actual component inventory.

rows.anchor: We now need to establish the actual boundary of KnowledgeOS before analyzing individual components. This distinction is essential because otherwise the architecture will gradually absorb every tool that touches the platform.
rows.statement: States the need to establish the actual KnowledgeOS boundary before component analysis, warning that without it the architecture would gradually absorb every tool that touches the platform.

rows.anchor: 110.1 — The system boundary rule ... K_OS={x | x has an evidenced architectural role in KnowledgeOS}. Not K_OS={x | x happens to interact with KnowledgeOS}. An external Git server may be essential to KnowledgeOS without becoming part of KnowledgeOS itself.
rows.statement: Defines K_OS={x | x has an evidenced architectural role in KnowledgeOS}, explicitly rejecting the weaker K_OS={x | x happens to interact with KnowledgeOS}.

rows.anchor: 110.2 — Six boundary classifications ... CORE, SUPPORTING, AGENT, EXTERNAL, LEGACY, UNKNOWN. This is intentionally conservative.
rows.statement: Defines six intentionally conservative boundary classifications: CORE, SUPPORTING, AGENT, EXTERNAL, LEGACY, UNKNOWN.

rows.anchor: 110.3 — CORE ... A component is CORE when removing it would remove an essential KnowledgeOS capability. Examples: KnowledgeModel, KnowledgePersistence, GovernanceEngine, EvidenceModel, if these actually exist in the implementation. But we must verify their existence.
rows.statement: Defines CORE as a component whose removal would remove an essential capability, listing candidate examples pending verification of actual existence.

rows.anchor: 110.4 — SUPPORTING ... Database, MessageBroker, ObjectStorage, CI/CD, Observability. Used by KnowledgeOS does not mean semantically part of KnowledgeOS.
rows.statement: Defines SUPPORTING infrastructure (Database/MessageBroker/ObjectStorage/CI-CD/Observability), stating usage does not entail semantic membership.

rows.anchor: 110.5 — AGENT ... .claude/, .codex/, AGENTS.md, agent hooks, agent commands, agent-specific settings. Their purpose is AgentBehavior. They become part of the broader ecosystem but should not automatically be classified as the KnowledgeOS semantic core.
rows.statement: Defines AGENT classification for .claude/.codex/AGENTS.md and agent hooks/commands/settings, ecosystem members not automatically semantic core.

rows.anchor: 110.6 — EXTERNAL ... GitHub, GitLab, Jira, CI, CloudProvider. Its data may become KnowledgeOS evidence, but the external system retains its own system boundary.
rows.statement: Defines EXTERNAL systems (GitHub/GitLab/Jira/CI/CloudProvider) that retain their own boundary even as their data becomes KnowledgeOS evidence.

rows.anchor: 110.7 — LEGACY ... old-memory-sync, old-registry, deprecated-indexer, legacy-agent-script. A repository containing an artifact does not mean the artifact belongs to the current architecture.
rows.statement: Defines LEGACY artifacts as especially dangerous for creating false architectural impressions, since repository presence does not entail current-architecture membership.

rows.anchor: 110.8 — UNKNOWN ... This is a legitimate result. It means we have not yet established enough evidence to classify the artifact. It does not mean External.
rows.statement: Defines UNKNOWN as a legitimate classification meaning insufficient evidence, explicitly distinct from External.

rows.anchor: 110.9 — Experiment 1 ... scripts/session-changes-logger. Is it Core, Supporting, Agent, External or Legacy? If invoked by agent hooks: likely AGENT/SUPPORTING. But classification awaits evidence. Result: UNKNOWN until usage is established
rows.statement: Experiment 1: session-changes-logger's classification (likely AGENT/SUPPORTING if hook-invoked) is UNKNOWN until usage evidence is established.

rows.anchor: 110.10 — Experiment 2 ... .claude/settings.json controls Claude execution. Expected: AGENT. It is not automatically CORE KnowledgeOS. Result: AGENT
rows.statement: Experiment 2: .claude/settings.json is classified AGENT, not automatically CORE KnowledgeOS.

rows.anchor: 110.11 — Experiment 3 ... A PostgreSQL database stores KnowledgeOS records. Expected: SUPPORTING unless the architecture explicitly defines the database as part of the deployable KnowledgeOS product boundary. Result: SUPPORTING
rows.statement: Experiment 3: a PostgreSQL database storing KnowledgeOS records is SUPPORTING unless explicitly defined as part of the deployable product boundary.

rows.anchor: 110.12 — Logical boundary versus deployment boundary ... A system may logically contain KnowledgeService while deployment uses PostgreSQL as an external managed service. LogicalBoundary≠DeploymentBoundary.
rows.statement: States LogicalBoundary≠DeploymentBoundary: a logical component may be deployed via an externally managed service.

rows.anchor: 110.13 — Product boundary versus ecosystem boundary ... Product boundary K_product, Ecosystem boundary K_ecosystem, External environment K_environment. K_product⊆K_ecosystem⊆K_environment.
rows.statement: Defines a three-tier boundary containment K_product⊆K_ecosystem⊆K_environment (Product/Ecosystem/External-environment boundaries).

rows.anchor: 110.14 — Example ... KnowledgeOS Ecosystem diagram: Core (Knowledge/Governance/Assurance), Claude/Codex/CI-CD agents, then GitHub/Jira/Cloud-Infra outer systems interacting without becoming core.
rows.statement: Presents a worked ecosystem diagram: KnowledgeOS Core surrounded by Claude/Codex/CI-CD, interacting with outer GitHub/Jira/Cloud-Infra systems without becoming core.

rows.anchor: 110.15 — Agent harness boundary ... This resolves an earlier architectural question. Claude and Codex are EcosystemParticipants. Their harnesses are AgentOperatingLayers. KnowledgeOS remains SemanticKnowledge+Governance+Evidence+Assurance according to the actual implementation.
rows.statement: Resolves the recurring agent-harness classification question: Claude/Codex are EcosystemParticipants with AgentOperatingLayers, while KnowledgeOS itself is SemanticKnowledge+Governance+Evidence+Assurance.

rows.anchor: 110.16 — Experiment 4 ... Codex reads KnowledgeOS architecture. Does that make Codex part of KnowledgeOS? Not necessarily. Expected: Codex=EcosystemParticipant. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 4: Codex reading KnowledgeOS architecture does not make it part of KnowledgeOS; it is classified EcosystemParticipant; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 110.17 — But the relationship must be explicit ... Codex-consumes->KnowledgeOS. And potentially Codex-produces->Evidence. This is more informative than simply placing Codex inside the same directory.
rows.statement: States the Codex-KnowledgeOS relationship should be modeled explicitly (consumes/produces), more informative than mere directory co-location.

rows.anchor: 110.18 — External knowledge sources ... Git, Jira, Confluence, documents, runtime systems. These should be modeled as KnowledgeSources. Not automatically as KnowledgeOS components.
rows.statement: Defines external ingestion sources (Git/Jira/Confluence/documents/runtime systems) as KnowledgeSources, not automatically KnowledgeOS components.

rows.anchor: 110.19 — Experiment 5 ... Jira contains a change ticket. KnowledgeOS imports it as evidence. Expected: Jira=EXTERNAL, JiraTicket=ExternalEvidenceSource. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 5: an imported Jira ticket is classified Jira=EXTERNAL, JiraTicket=ExternalEvidenceSource; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 110.20 — Source authority ... External systems may remain authoritative for certain facts. Jira→ChangeRequestAuthority. KnowledgeOS may preserve a representation: KnowledgeOS→Reference/Projection. This distinction prevents duplicate authority.
rows.statement: States external systems may retain authority over certain facts while KnowledgeOS holds only a Reference/Projection, preventing duplicate authority.

rows.anchor: 110.21 — Experiment 6 ... Jira is authoritative for ticket status. KnowledgeOS stores ticket_status. Expected: KnowledgeOS should not silently become a competing authority unless explicitly designed to do so. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 6: KnowledgeOS storing a Jira-authoritative ticket_status field must not silently become a competing authority; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 110.22 — Projection versus ownership ... Projection≠Ownership. KnowledgeOS may contain Projection(X) without owning Truth(X). This is particularly important for evidence.
rows.statement: States Projection≠Ownership: holding Projection(X) does not entail owning Truth(X), important for evidence handling.

rows.anchor: 110.23 — Evidence source graph ... Source→Observation→KnowledgeOS. Git→Commit→Observation→KnowledgeOS Evidence.
rows.statement: Defines the evidence source graph Source→Observation→KnowledgeOS, illustrated by Git→Commit→Observation→KnowledgeOS Evidence.

rows.anchor: 110.24 — Experiment 7 ... Git commit is imported. Expected: KnowledgeOS records source, commit identity, timestamp, repository, relationship to observed change. Result: PASS if implemented. The architectural requirement is clear; implementation remains to be evidenced.
rows.statement: Experiment 7: importing a Git commit should record source/commit identity/timestamp/repository/relationship to change; result conditionally PASS pending implementation evidence.

rows.anchor: 110.25 — Boundary discovery through dependency direction ... DependencyDirection. If A→B we ask: which system owns the contract? The caller is not necessarily the owner.
rows.statement: States boundary discovery via dependency direction: for A→B, contract ownership must be determined separately, since the caller is not necessarily the owner.

rows.anchor: 110.26 — Experiment 8 ... KnowledgeOS calls GitHub API. Expected: GitHub=External. KnowledgeOS is the consumer. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 8: KnowledgeOS calling the GitHub API leaves GitHub=External with KnowledgeOS as consumer; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 110.27 — Reverse integration ... If GitHub webhook calls KnowledgeOS: GitHub remains external. The direction of invocation does not determine system ownership.
rows.statement: States the direction of invocation does not determine system ownership: a GitHub-initiated webhook still leaves GitHub external.

rows.anchor: 110.28 — Experiment 9 ... GitHub sends an event to KnowledgeOS. Expected: GitHub=EXTERNAL, KnowledgeOS=CORE. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 9: an inbound GitHub event still leaves GitHub=EXTERNAL, KnowledgeOS=CORE; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 110.29 — Infrastructure boundary ... Podman, Kubernetes, Docker, PostgreSQL, Redis, Kafka may be essential to operation. But InfrastructureDependency≠KnowledgeModel.
rows.statement: States InfrastructureDependency≠KnowledgeModel: operational essentiality of infrastructure tools does not make them semantic components.

rows.anchor: 110.30 — Experiment 10 ... KnowledgeOS cannot run without PostgreSQL. Expected: PostgreSQL is operationally essential but not automatically a KnowledgeOS semantic component. Result: SUPPORTING
rows.statement: Experiment 10: PostgreSQL, though operationally essential, is classified SUPPORTING rather than a semantic component.

rows.anchor: 110.31 — Runtime boundary ... A runtime process may be part of KnowledgeOS even if its source resides elsewhere. Conversely, source code may exist in the repository but never participate in the current runtime. RuntimeMembership must be separately established.
rows.statement: States RuntimeMembership must be separately established from source-code presence, since runtime and repository membership can diverge in either direction.

rows.anchor: 110.32 — Experiment 11 ... A repository contains legacy-indexer/. It is not deployed. Expected: LEGACY or UNKNOWN. Not CORE RuntimeComponent. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 11: an undeployed legacy-indexer/ is classified LEGACY or UNKNOWN, never CORE RuntimeComponent; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 110.33 — The 'dead code' problem ... experimental code, abandoned prototypes, old migrations, historical scripts, unused libraries. RepositoryMembership≠SystemMembership. This is one of the most important findings of the reconstruction methodology.
rows.statement: States RepositoryMembership≠SystemMembership as one of the reconstruction methodology's most important findings, given repositories' accumulation of experimental/abandoned/unused code.

rows.anchor: 110.34 — Experiment 12 ... A module has 5,000 lines of sophisticated knowledge code. No build references it. Expected: it cannot be counted as operational KnowledgeOS functionality. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 12: a substantial but build-unreferenced module cannot be counted as operational functionality; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 110.35 — Build graph ... BuildGraph. Is the module compiled? Is it packaged? Is it included in deployment? Is it referenced? Is it tested? This gives stronger evidence of actual membership.
rows.statement: Defines the BuildGraph inspection (compiled/packaged/included/referenced/tested) as stronger evidence of actual system membership.

rows.anchor: 110.36 — Experiment 13 ... Module is compiled but never deployed. Expected: IMPLEMENTED but NOT OPERATIONAL. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 13: a compiled-but-never-deployed module is IMPLEMENTED but NOT OPERATIONAL; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 110.37 — Deployment graph ... DeploymentGraph. Repository→BuildArtifact→Container→Deployment→Runtime. Only components with an established path should be treated as operational.
rows.statement: Defines the DeploymentGraph Repository→BuildArtifact→Container→Deployment→Runtime as the required path for operational status.

rows.anchor: 110.38 — Experiment 14 ... Source component exists. No build artifact contains it. Expected: NonOperational. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 14: a source component absent from any build artifact is NonOperational; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 110.39 — Runtime graph ... RuntimeGraph. A component is operationally part of the system if we can establish Artifact→Deployment→RuntimeInstance.
rows.statement: Defines the RuntimeGraph criterion Artifact→Deployment→RuntimeInstance for establishing operational membership.

rows.anchor: 110.40 — Experiment 15 ... Deployment manifest contains service X. Runtime never starts it. Expected: DeploymentDefined but RuntimeNotObserved. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 15: a manifest-defined but never-started service is DeploymentDefined/RuntimeNotObserved; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 110.41 — Boundary confidence ... Confidence∈{High,Medium,Low}. CoreComponent+BuildEvidence+RuntimeEvidence⇒High.
rows.statement: Defines a three-level boundary-classification confidence scale (High/Medium/Low), with the composition rule CoreComponent+BuildEvidence+RuntimeEvidence⇒High.

rows.anchor: 110.42 — Boundary evidence record ... BoundaryEvidence=(Classification,Reason,Evidence,Confidence,Date). This prevents later arguments based on memory.
rows.statement: Defines the BoundaryEvidence=(Classification,Reason,Evidence,Confidence,Date) record schema, preventing later memory-based disputes over classification.

type_signature.codomain: Classification x Reason x Evidence x Confidence x Date

rows.anchor: 110.43 — Experiment 16 ... Someone later asks why .claude/ is classified as agent-specific. Expected: KnowledgeOS can point to configuration semantics, invocation, hooks, agent-specific behavior. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 16: a later classification challenge (.claude/ as agent-specific) must be answerable by pointing to configuration semantics/invocation/hooks/behavior; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 110.44 — Context map ... DDD-style context map: KnowledgeOS (Knowledge/Governance/Evidence/Assurance) surrounded by Claude/Codex/CI-CD, then External Sources (Git/Tickets/Documents/Runtime). This is the logical ecosystem map, not yet the final physical topology.
rows.statement: Presents a DDD-style logical ecosystem context map (KnowledgeOS core, Claude/Codex/CI-CD, external Git/Tickets/Documents/Runtime), explicitly not yet the final physical topology.

rows.anchor: 110.45 — Upstream/downstream relationships ... For each external interaction we should determine Upstream and Downstream. Git→KnowledgeOS may mean Git is upstream for source evidence.
rows.statement: States per-interaction upstream/downstream determination is required, illustrated by Git as upstream source-evidence provider.

rows.anchor: 110.46 — Experiment 17 ... KnowledgeOS publishes a governance result into Jira. KnowledgeOS→Jira. Jira is downstream for that interaction. The same external system can therefore be Upstream for one relationship and Downstream for another.
rows.statement: Experiment 17: Jira, upstream as an evidence source, becomes downstream when KnowledgeOS publishes a governance result into it, showing the same system can hold both roles across relationships.

rows.anchor: 110.47 — Relationship semantics ... We should avoid generic 'integrates with.' Instead classify relationships: Consumes, Produces, Reads, Writes, Publishes, Subscribes, Verifies, Authorizes, Projects. This makes the context map executable.
rows.statement: Defines a nine-verb relationship-semantics vocabulary (Consumes/Produces/Reads/Writes/Publishes/Subscribes/Verifies/Authorizes/Projects) replacing generic 'integrates with' phrasing, making the context map executable.

rows.anchor: 110.48 — Experiment 18 ... Codex reads architecture knowledge and writes code. Expected: Codex-consumes->KnowledgeOS and Codex-produces->EngineeringChange. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 18: Codex's activity is modeled as Codex-consumes->KnowledgeOS and Codex-produces->EngineeringChange; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 110.49 — System boundary invariants ... I_Boundary: a component must not be classified as Core solely because it is stored in the same repository. I_AuthorityBoundary: data projection does not automatically transfer authority. I_RuntimeMembership: source existence does not establish runtime membersh
rows.statement: Names five system-boundary invariants: I_Boundary, I_AuthorityBoundary, I_RuntimeMembership, I_AgentBoundary, I_External.

invariants.name: I_Boundary
invariants.statement: A component must not be classified as Core solely because it is stored in the same repository.

invariants.name: I_AuthorityBoundary
invariants.statement: Data projection does not automatically transfer authority.

invariants.name: I_RuntimeMembership
invariants.statement: Source existence does not establish runtime membership.

invariants.name: I_AgentBoundary
invariants.statement: Agent-specific operating artifacts must remain distinguishable from authoritative KnowledgeOS knowledge.

invariants.name: I_External
invariants.statement: External systems remain externally owned unless explicit system-boundary evidence establishes otherwise.

rows.anchor: 110.50 — The first actual system map ... Organizational Governance/Intent → KNOWLEDGEOS (Knowledge/Evidence/Governance/Assurance/Semantic Relationships) → Claude Agent/Codex Agent/Engineering Systems → External Knowledge Sources → Git/Jira/Runtime. The exact components inside each box remain an empi
rows.statement: Presents the first actual system map diagram from Organizational Governance/Intent through KnowledgeOS core, agent/engineering layers, to external knowledge sources, with exact box contents flagged as still empirical.

rows.anchor: 110.51 — What Step 110 has established ... We have established the boundary method, not yet the final component list. The important result is that we now know how to decide whether an artifact belongs to Core versus Ecosystem versus External.
rows.statement: States Step 110 establishes the boundary-classification method, not the final component list, having established how to decide Core vs Ecosystem vs External membership.

rows.anchor: 110.52 — Step 110 verdict: STEP 110 — SYSTEM BOUNDARY MODEL: PASS. The conceptual boundary is coherent. The empirical boundary remains KnowledgeOS_ActualBoundary=TBD until the repository and operational evidence are mapped.
rows.statement: Records Step 110 verdict PASS for conceptual boundary coherence, with the honest empirical verdict KnowledgeOS_ActualBoundary=TBD pending repository/operational evidence mapping.

rows.anchor: 110.53 — The next step: Step 111 — Actual Component Inventory. Component→Responsibility→Data→Behavior→Interface→Dependency→Evidence→Runtime. Is there actually one coherent KnowledgeOS core, or has the current implementation evolved into several partially overlapping subsystems? That question will be
rows.statement: Previews Step 111: reconstructing the real internal architecture via Component→Responsibility→Data→Behavior→Interface→Dependency→Evidence→Runtime, centered on whether KnowledgeOS is one coherent core or several partially overlapping subsystems.

lexical.anchor: We now need to establish the actual boundary of KnowledgeOS before analyzing individual components. This distinction is essential because otherwise the architecture will gradually absorb every tool that touches the platform.

formal.anchor: 110.1 — The system boundary rule ... K_OS={x | x has an evidenced architectural role in KnowledgeOS}. Not K_OS={x | x happens to interact with KnowledgeOS}. An external Git server may be essential to KnowledgeOS without becoming part of KnowledgeOS itself.

operational.anchor: 110.9 — Experiment 1 ... scripts/session-changes-logger. Is it Core, Supporting, Agent, External or Legacy? If invoked by agent hooks: likely AGENT/SUPPORTING. But classification awaits evidence. Result: UNKNOWN until usage is established

aliases: Step 24: Formal Composition, Consistency, Invariants, and Closure of the KnowledgeOS Model

sources.note: S0880's Step 24, a verification/stress-test step: resolves the apparent Knowledge->Action->Outcome->Knowledge circularity via temporal indexing; verifies eleven consistency properties; states the KnowledgeOS Closure Principle (seven properties preserved per governed cycle) with Closure!=Correctness; defines four execution classes and four reasons a result can be unavailable; consolidates C1-C20 Core Invariants; verdicts the model COMPOSABLE while declining to claim computability is proven; hands off to Step 25 (executable reference model / adversarial simulation).

rows.anchor: Up to Step 23 we have deliberately built the vocabulary and mathematical components. Step 24 changes our method: We stop adding concepts and try to break the model. Do all concepts we have defined actually compose into one coherent computational system?
rows.statement: Announces a methodological shift at Step 24: stop adding concepts and instead test whether everything defined so far actually composes into one coherent computational system.

rows.anchor: The complete KnowledgeOS transformation ... \mathcal M: (S,K,G,E,D,A,O) \rightarrow (S',K',G',E',D',A',O') ... S \rightarrow Observation \rightarrow E \rightarrow K \rightarrow Decision \rightarrow A \rightarrow S' followed by S' \rightarrow Observation \rightarrow E' \rightarrow K'. This gives us a
rows.statement: Models the whole system as a state-transition system M over (WorldState,Knowledge,Goals,Evidence,Decisions,Actions,Outcomes), assembling the closed feedback loop S→Observation→E→K→Decision→A→S'→....

rows.anchor: But closure is not enough ... TypeConsistency, SemanticConsistency, TemporalConsistency, IdentityConsistency, EvidencePreservation, UncertaintyPreservation, ProvenancePreservation, GovernanceConsistency, Computability, Termination, Failure Representability.
rows.statement: Lists eleven consistency properties the model must be verified against beyond mere closure: Type/Semantic/Temporal/Identity Consistency, Evidence/Uncertainty/Provenance Preservation, Governance Consistency, Computability, Termination, Failure Representability.

rows.anchor: First verification: type consistency ... Observation: S\rightarrow E ... Assessment: E\rightarrow AssertionAssessment ... Commitment: AssertionAssessment\rightarrow K ... Reasoning: K\rightarrow DerivedKnowledge ... Zero: (K,I)\rightarrow \Delta ... Lord: (\Delta,G,K)\rightarrow\mathcal A ... Sārath
rows.statement: Verifies type consistency by chaining all ten major transformations' input/output types end to end, noting any undefined type boundary would fail the model.

rows.anchor: Type closure ... \forall x\in Domain(f),\quad f(x)\in Y. ... an LLM cannot directly produce CommittedKnowledge unless the commitment boundary explicitly permits it. LLMOutput \not\rightarrow CommittedKnowledge by default. Instead LLMOutput \rightarrow CandidateAssertion \rightarrow Assessment \right
rows.statement: States the type-closure requirement ∀x∈Domain(f), f(x)∈Y, applied to forbid LLMOutput→CommittedKnowledge by default, requiring the full CandidateAssertion→Assessment→Commitment path.

rows.anchor: Composition ... Observation \rightarrow Evidence \rightarrow Knowledge. And Knowledge \rightarrow Discrepancy \rightarrow Action. And Action \rightarrow Outcome \rightarrow Evidence.
rows.statement: Verifies functions compose as expected across the three major sub-chains (Observation→Evidence→Knowledge; Knowledge→Discrepancy→Action; Action→Outcome→Evidence).

rows.anchor: The critical circularity ... Knowledge \rightarrow Action \rightarrow Outcome \rightarrow Knowledge. Is this a mathematical contradiction? No. It is a state transition loop. K_t \xrightarrow{Action} S_{t+1} \xrightarrow{Observation} K_{t+1}. The time index prevents the circularity from becoming an a
rows.statement: Resolves the apparent Knowledge→Action→Outcome→Knowledge circularity: it is a temporally-indexed state transition loop (K_t→K_{t+1}), not an algebraic self-reference (K_t→K_t) — no contradiction.

rows.anchor: Temporal closure ... Knowledge Update must be temporally ordered. If an event occurs at t_1 and is observed at t_2>t_1, then K_{t_2} may incorporate that observation. It must not silently modify K_{t_0} for t_0<t_1. ... Historical knowledge ... K_t=T(K_0,e_1,\ldots,e_t). This is one of the most impo
rows.statement: States Knowledge Update must be temporally ordered — a later observation may update K_{t2} but must never silently modify an earlier K_{t0} — requiring historical reconstructibility K_t=T(K_0,e_1,...,e_t).

rows.anchor: Identity consistency ... Identity(E,t_1)=Identity(E,t_2) unless there is an explicit identity transition. StateChange\neq IdentityChange. ... Identity contradiction ... FQDN\rightarrow E_1 and FQDN\rightarrow E_2. KnowledgeOS must not silently choose one. It must create IdentityConflict.
rows.statement: States Identity(E,t1)=Identity(E,t2) absent an explicit identity transition (StateChange≠IdentityChange), and requires an explicit IdentityConflict object rather than silently choosing between contradictory identity claims.

rows.anchor: Evidence conservation ... E\rightarrow A, the conclusion must retain a reference to E. DerivedKnowledge \Rightarrow TraceableEvidence. We should never have "KnowledgeOS believes X" without being able to determine why. ... Evidence conservation does not mean every conclusion needs raw evidence ... A_
rows.statement: States DerivedKnowledge⇒TraceableEvidence — every conclusion must reference its evidence, and lineage chains must eventually terminate in provenance-bearing inputs (or explicit axioms/normative premises).

rows.anchor: Axioms are special ... x+y=y+x within a mathematical structure. Or an organizational constitution may establish: Production changes require approval. OriginType\in\{Observation,Normative,Axiom,Definition,Derived,HumanDecision\}. This prevents us from forcing all knowledge into empirical evidence.
rows.statement: Defines a six-value OriginType enum {Observation,Normative,Axiom,Definition,Derived,HumanDecision}, explicitly preventing forcing all knowledge into empirical evidence.

rows.anchor: Uncertainty preservation ... x\in[10,20]. A transformation must not silently produce x=15. unless there is a valid inference rule. Transformation must preserve epistemic information. ... False precision ... No transformation may increase precision without justification. Date\approx August cannot bec
rows.statement: States transformations must preserve epistemic information — no unjustified precision increase, illustrated by an interval [10,20] that must not silently become a point value, and an approximate date that must not become exact merely from an LLM guess.

rows.anchor: Uncertainty monotonicity ... KnowledgeOS does not require uncertainty to monotonically decrease. New evidence can increase uncertainty. Initially A appears certain. New evidence reveals A\lor B. The epistemic state becomes more uncertain. Knowledge acquisition need not monotonically reduce uncertain
rows.statement: Corrects any assumption of monotonic uncertainty reduction or knowledge growth: new evidence can increase uncertainty, and a committed assertion can later be retracted (A∈K_t, A∉K_{t+1}) — this is epistemic revision, not inconsistency.

rows.anchor: Belief revision ... Revision as a first-class operation. Revise(K,E_{new}) \rightarrow K'. The revision must preserve reason; evidence; temporal position; affected dependencies.
rows.statement: Requires Revision be a first-class operation Revise(K,E_new)→K' preserving reason, evidence, temporal position, and affected dependencies.

rows.anchor: Dependency consistency ... If A is retracted, KnowledgeOS must determine whether B remains valid. Retracting a premise triggers dependency analysis. It does not necessarily automatically invalidate every descendant. ... Why not automatically delete descendants? ... If A is retracted but C independen
rows.statement: States retracting a premise triggers dependency analysis (not automatic deletion) — a descendant supported by an independent second premise may survive retraction of one, requiring re-evaluation not blind deletion.

rows.anchor: Provenance closure ... Every committed assertion should be traceable to origin; transformation; assessor; authority; time; policy. Provenance(CommittedKnowledge)\neq\varnothing for governed knowledge.
rows.statement: States Provenance(CommittedKnowledge)≠∅ — every committed assertion must be traceable to origin, transformation, assessor, authority, time, and policy.

rows.anchor: Governance closure ... Action \Rightarrow Authorization for governed actions. If Authorization=Unknown, the system must not convert it to Authorized=True. ... Safety invariant ... UnknownAuthorization \not\Rightarrow Authorization. And RejectedAuthorization \Rightarrow NoExecution. This is a critica
rows.statement: States governed actions require authorization; UnknownAuthorization must never become Authorization, and RejectedAuthorization must always block execution — a critical safety boundary.

rows.anchor: Decision consistency ... D_t=f(K_t,\Pi_t). If later K_{t+1} changes, that does not mean D_t was irrational. It means the information state changed. ... Decision invalidation ... if A\in Dependencies(D), then Change(A) should trigger Review(D). KnowledgeChange \rightarrow PotentialDecisionReview.
rows.statement: States a later knowledge change does not retroactively make an earlier decision irrational (D_t=f(K_t,Π_t) evaluated at its own time), but a change to a decision's dependency should trigger PotentialDecisionReview.

rows.anchor: Idempotency ... Process(E) and again Process(E). We do not want duplicate knowledge artifacts. f(f(x))=f(x) where semantically appropriate. RegisterEvidence(E) should be idempotent based on evidence identity. ... Not every operation is idempotent ... IncrementCounter is not idempotent. Likewise Depl
rows.statement: Requires operations like RegisterEvidence be idempotent (f(f(x))=f(x)) based on evidence identity, while others (IncrementCounter, Deploy) are not — idempotency is operation-specific and must be explicitly declared.

rows.anchor: Determinism ... Hash(x) or ValidateSchema(x). Given identical inputs f(x)=f(x). Other processes may be nondeterministic, especially LLM generation. Determinism must be explicit per operation. ... LLM nondeterminism ... CandidateAssertion_1 on one execution and CandidateAssertion_2 on another. This d
rows.statement: Requires determinism be declared explicitly per operation, with LLM nondeterminism confined to a CandidateGeneration boundary, followed by deterministic assessment where possible.

rows.anchor: Semantic consistency ... A word must mean the same thing inside its bounded context. Evidence must not mean source document in one context and validated truth in another. UbiquitousLanguage must be context bounded. ... Bounded-context translation ... ExternalDocument \xrightarrow{Translation} Candid
rows.statement: Requires Ubiquitous Language be context-bounded (a term like 'Evidence' must mean the same thing within one bounded context), with explicit traceable translation across contexts to prevent semantic leakage.

rows.anchor: Aggregate invariants ... Evidence aggregate Cannot exist without SourceReference or explicit origin type. Decision aggregate Cannot transition to Approved without required authority. Action aggregate Cannot transition to Executing without execution prerequisites. This is where DDD becomes computatio
rows.statement: Gives three worked aggregate invariants (Evidence requires SourceReference/origin type, Decision cannot reach Approved without authority, Action cannot reach Executing without prerequisites), where DDD becomes computationally useful.

rows.anchor: State machines ... For Evidence: Captured \rightarrow Assessed \rightarrow Accepted/Rejected. For Knowledge: Candidate \rightarrow Supported \rightarrow Committed or Candidate \rightarrow Disputed. For Decision: Proposed \rightarrow Reviewed \rightarrow Approved/Rejected. For Action: Planned \righta
rows.statement: Defines explicit state machines for Evidence, Knowledge, Decision, and Action lifecycles, requiring illegal transitions (e.g. CandidateAction→Executing without authorization) be formally rejected — making governance computational.

rows.anchor: Failure states ... EvidenceAcquisitionFailed, IdentityResolutionFailed, AssessmentFailed, DecisionNotReady, AuthorizationDenied, ExecutionFailed, OutcomeUnknown. These are not exceptions that disappear into logs. They are domain states/events.
rows.statement: Requires seven named failure states be represented as first-class domain states/events, never exceptions that disappear into logs.

rows.anchor: Partial failure ... E_1,E_2,E_3,E_4,E_5. But E_4 is unavailable. KnowledgeOS should not necessarily fail the entire operation. EvidenceAvailability=\{E_1,E_2,E_3,E_5\} and E_4=Unavailable. Then sufficiency is reevaluated. ... Graceful degradation ... Failure of one information source \neq Failure of
rows.statement: Requires graceful degradation on partial evidence-source failure (Failure of one source ≠ Failure of the entire process) unless the missing source is contextually critical, in which case Ready may still become False.

rows.anchor: Termination ... Can KnowledgeOS get stuck investigating forever? Lord \rightarrow InformationAction \rightarrow NewEvidence \rightarrow MoreUncertainty \rightarrow MoreInformationAction \rightarrow\cdots This is a possible infinite loop. ... Termination policy ... Ready=True or NoUsefulActionRemaini
rows.statement: Warns of a possible infinite investigation loop (Lord→InformationAction→NewEvidence→MoreUncertainty→...), requiring an explicit termination policy with four stopping conditions (Ready, NoUsefulActionRemaining, BudgetExceeded, HumanEscalationRequired) — the system needs a stopping policy, not a proof every investigation terminates.

rows.anchor: Computability boundary ... Is every operation in our model computable? No—and we should not pretend otherwise. Algorithmically computable. Others depend on ExternalReality. Others require HumanJudgment. Others involve ProbabilisticInference. Others use LLM approximation. The correct goal is not: Eve
rows.statement: Honestly states not every operation is computable, reframing the goal from 'everything is automatically computable' to 'every operation has an explicitly defined computational or non-computational boundary'.

rows.anchor: Four execution classes ... C=\{Deterministic,Probabilistic,AI-Assisted,Human-Governed\}. Every major operation should belong to one or more classes. ... Deterministic ... schema validation; identity matching under exact rules; temporal ordering; hashing; dependency traversal; readiness predicates; c
rows.statement: Defines four execution classes (Deterministic, Probabilistic, AI-Assisted, Human-Governed) that every major operation must be classified into, each with concrete examples, and requires human judgment never be disguised as deterministic computation.

rows.anchor: This resolves an earlier concern ... Can we compute everything? We can formally represent and govern every operation, but not every operation is algorithmically decidable. That is a much stronger and more honest claim. ... Mathematical undecidability ... KnowledgeOS must always determine the truth o
rows.statement: Reframes the recurring 'can everything be computed' question into 'every operation can be formally represented and governed, but not every operation is algorithmically decidable', requiring KnowledgeOS represent Undetermined explicitly.

rows.anchor: Incomplete information versus undecidability ... Incomplete We lack required information. Undecidable under the model No algorithm within the formal system can determine the result. Computationally infeasible A solution may exist but be impractical to compute. Human-governed The result requires an a
rows.statement: Distinguishes four different reasons a determination may be unavailable: Incomplete (missing info), Undecidable-under-the-model, Computationally infeasible (exists but impractical), and Human-governed — all four must be kept distinct.

rows.anchor: Complexity ... O(n) versus O(2^n). Our model must eventually track ComplexityClass or at least ComputationalCost. This becomes relevant when KnowledgeOS scales to millions of evidence relationships. ... Graph scalability ... Traceability queries over G=(V,E) may be computationally manageable for loc
rows.statement: Notes computational complexity (e.g. O(n) vs O(2^n)) matters at scale, requiring traceability queries have depth limits, scope, relation filters, and time boundaries rather than unrestricted transitive closure.

rows.anchor: Conservation of semantics ... summarization may preserve Meaning but not FullEvidence. Therefore a summary cannot replace the original evidence. Summary \rightarrow SourceArtifact through provenance. ... Compression is not lossless ... Information(Summary) < Information(Document). DerivedSummary\neq
rows.statement: States DerivedSummary ≠ SourceEvidence (a summary cannot replace the original since Information(Summary)<Information(Document)), requiring transformations declare an InformationLossProfile so KnowledgeOS knows when it must return to the original source.

rows.anchor: Retrieval is not knowledge acquisition by itself ... A document retrieved from the Internet gives RetrievedArtifact. It does not automatically become Knowledge. Retrieval \rightarrow EvidenceCandidate \rightarrow Assessment \rightarrow Knowledge. This preserves Step 19. ... RAG versus KnowledgeOS ..
rows.statement: Restates RetrievedArtifact ⇏ Knowledge (must pass through EvidenceCandidate→Assessment), contrasting conventional RAG's Query→Retrieve→Generate with KnowledgeOS's eight-stage Query→Retrieve→Assess→Interpret→Validate→Commit→Reason→Respond pipeline plus a five-stage action extension.

rows.anchor: Composition test ... F=Observe\circ Assess\circ Commit\circ Reason\circ Zero\circ Lord\circ Sārathi\circ Govern\circ Execute. The more correct representation is K_{t+1}=T_K(K_t,Observe(Execute(Decision(Lord(Zero(K_t)))))). This demonstrates that the system is mathematically composable.
rows.statement: Tests full-cycle function composition, giving the more accurate event-driven stateful form K_{t+1}=T_K(K_t,Observe(Execute(Decision(Lord(Zero(K_t)))))) demonstrating mathematical composability.

rows.anchor: But there is a hidden dependency ... Zero requires IdealState. Zero(K) is meaningless without a selected goal/purpose or ideal state. Zero(K,G) is more accurate than Zero(K). ... Lord also requires intent ... Lord(\Delta) is insufficient. Lord(\Delta,G,K,C) \rightarrow CandidateActions. ... Sārathi
rows.statement: Corrects earlier under-specified signatures for Zero, Lord, Sārathi, and Authorization — each requires explicit Goal/Constraints/Policy/Context arguments (Zero(K,G), Lord(Δ,G,K,C), Sārathi(K,G,A,C,Π), Authorize(D,Role,Context,t)), a hidden dependency the model had glossed over.

rows.anchor: The corrected complete chain ... Observation \rightarrow Evidence ... Evidence+Context \rightarrow Assessment ... Assessment+Policy \rightarrow Knowledge ... Knowledge+Goal+IdealState \rightarrow Discrepancy ... Discrepancy+Goal+Constraints \rightarrow CandidateActions ... CandidateActions+Knowledge
rows.statement: Assembles the corrected complete chain with every hidden dependency made explicit, called a much cleaner mathematical architecture than earlier under-specified versions.

rows.anchor: The major closure theorem ... KnowledgeOS Closure Principle ... K_t \rightarrow Decision_t \rightarrow Action_t \rightarrow Outcome_t \rightarrow Evidence_{t+1} \rightarrow K_{t+1}, the resulting knowledge state must preserve Identity + TemporalContext + Evidence + Provenance + Uncertainty + Decisio
rows.statement: States the KnowledgeOS Closure Principle: every governed action cycle must preserve seven properties (Identity, TemporalContext, Evidence, Provenance, Uncertainty, DecisionLineage, Governance) — losing any one means the loop is not closed.

rows.anchor: Closure does not mean truth preservation ... A closed system can preserve provenance while still reaching an incorrect conclusion. Closure\neq Correctness. We need a separate correctness/validation analysis. ... Correctness layers ... Syntactic correctness Is the object structurally valid? Semantic
rows.statement: States Closure ≠ Correctness (a closed system can still reach an incorrect conclusion), defining a four-layer Correctness model: Syntactic, Semantic, Epistemic, and Operational correctness.

rows.anchor: Statistical correctness ... StatisticalValidity including calibration; sampling assumptions; independence; model assumptions; uncertainty intervals; validation. A numerically correct computation can still be statistically invalid if its assumptions are wrong. ... Architectural correctness ... Archit
rows.statement: Adds StatisticalValidity (calibration, sampling, independence, model assumptions) as a fifth correctness dimension for statistical components, and ArchitectureCorrectness (boundaries/invariants/valid transitions) at the system level, where DDD and mathematical modeling converge.

rows.anchor: The model is now testable ... Test 1 LLM output cannot directly become committed knowledge. Test 2 Unknown authorization blocks execution. Test 3 Retracting evidence triggers dependency analysis. Test 4 Historical decision uses historical knowledge snapshot. Test 5 Duplicate evidence registration is
rows.statement: Derives ten concrete executable tests directly from the theory's invariants, marking the point where the theory becomes testable engineering.

rows.anchor: Property-based testing ... Register(E);Register(E) = Register(E). For every committed assertion A: Trace(A) must reach provenance. For every unauthorized action a: Execute(a)=Denied. For every historical decision D_t: Dependencies(D_t)\subseteq K_t or explicitly declared external inputs. This is mat
rows.statement: Formulates four universally-quantified property-based tests (idempotent registration, provenance-reaching traceability, denied unauthorized execution, decision dependencies contained in the historical snapshot) as mathematical property testing.

rows.anchor: Model checking ... Candidate \rightarrow Committed may be allowed. But Rejected \rightarrow Executing should be impossible. \neg\exists transition: Rejected\rightarrow Executing. This is amenable to formal verification techniques.
rows.statement: Frames illegal state transitions (e.g. Rejected→Executing) as a formally verifiable model-checking property ¬∃transition:Rejected→Executing.

rows.anchor: Invariant hierarchy ... Domain invariants What the business/domain permits. Epistemic invariants What valid knowledge representation requires. Architectural invariants What the system must enforce. This distinction is valuable for DDD.
rows.statement: Classifies invariants into three tiers — Domain (business permits), Epistemic (valid knowledge representation), Architectural (system enforcement) — valuable for DDD.

rows.anchor: Step 24 consolidated invariant set ... C1 Type closure ... C2 Temporal integrity ... C3 Identity integrity ... C4 Evidence conservation ... C5 Provenance conservation ... C6 Uncertainty conservation ... C7 Conflict preservation ... C8 Authority separation ... C9 Governance safety ... C10 Historical
rows.statement: Freezes twenty KnowledgeOS Core Invariants C1-C20 spanning type closure, temporal/identity integrity, evidence/provenance/uncertainty conservation, conflict preservation, authority separation, governance safety, historical reproducibility, revision traceability, explicit nondeterminism/uncertainty, termination, failure representation, contextual semantics, no false causality/probability/completeness, and outcome feedback — the consolidated candidate constitution to date.

rows.anchor: Step 24 verdict ... THE KNOWLEDGEOS CORE MODEL IS COMPOSABLE. We have not found a fundamental mathematical contradiction between the major components. Identity \leftrightarrow Time \leftrightarrow Evidence \leftrightarrow Knowledge \leftrightarrow Uncertainty \leftrightarrow Decision \leftrightarrow
rows.statement: Delivers the Step 24 verdict: the KnowledgeOS core model IS COMPOSABLE — no fundamental mathematical contradiction found across eight major stress-tested concept pairs, without collapsing fundamentally different concepts into one object.

rows.anchor: But I would not yet declare the mathematics completely closed ... We have proven architectural composability at the conceptual level. We have not yet demonstrated implementation-level computability for every operator. Formal Specification \rightarrow Executable Model \rightarrow Simulation \rightarr
rows.statement: Explicitly declines to declare the mathematics fully closed: architectural composability at the conceptual level has been proven, but implementation-level computability per operator has not; the next phase is Formal Specification→Executable Model→Simulation→Counterexample→Refinement, endorsing the criterion 'if we cannot compute it, the model is not finished'.

rows.anchor: Therefore I would change our methodology now ... Until Step 24 ... Conceptual Construction. From Step 25 onward ... Mathematical Verification and Experimental Falsification. We should stop assuming that the definitions work. We should try to break them.
rows.statement: Declares a methodology shift: Steps 1-24 were Conceptual Construction; from Step 25 onward, the project shifts to Mathematical Verification and Experimental Falsification — trying to break the definitions rather than assuming they work.

rows.anchor: Step 25 — Executable KnowledgeOS Reference Model and Adversarial Simulation ... construct a small but complete artificial world containing perhaps 5 entities; 10 observations; 15 evidence items; conflicting sources; temporal changes; ambiguous identity; uncertain measurements; an LLM-generated asser
rows.statement: Poses Step 25: build a small complete artificial world (specified entity/evidence/decision counts) and run the full Reality→Observation→...→NewKnowledge cycle while deliberately injecting ten adversarial failure conditions (missing data, contradictions, staleness, duplication, hallucination, identity collision, unauthorized action, execution failure, unexpected outcome, revised evidence), aiming to produce a computationally testable KnowledgeOS kernel specification if it survives.

lineage_claims.quote: Step 25 -- Executable KnowledgeOS Reference Model and Adversarial Simulation

experiment.hypothesis: The composed KnowledgeOS model can withstand adversarial injection of realistic failure modes across a small complete artificial world.
experiment.setup: 5 entities, 10 observations, 15 evidence items, conflicting sources, temporal changes, ambiguous identity, uncertain measurements, an LLM assertion, an ADR, a constitution rule, one discrepancy, three candidate actions, one authorization decision, one executed action, one unexpected outcome.
experiment.assumptions: The full Reality->Observation->...->NewKnowledge cycle can be run computationally over this small world.

S \rightarrow Observation \rightarrow E \rightarrow K \rightarrow Decision \rightarrow A \rightarrow S' followed by S' \rightarrow Observation \rightarrow E' \rightarrow K'. This gives us a
