rationale_evidence.anchor: The critical circularity ... Knowledge \rightarrow Action \rightarrow Outcome \rightarrow Knowledge. Is this a mathematical contradiction? No. It is a state transition loop. K_t \xrightarrow{Action} S_{t+1} \xrightarrow{Observation} K_{t+1}. The time index prevents the circularity from becoming an a
rationale_evidence.statement: Resolves the apparent Knowledge→Action→Outcome→Knowledge circularity: it is a temporally-indexed state transition loop (K_t→K_{t+1}), not an algebraic self-reference (K_t→K_t) — no contradiction.

rationale_evidence.anchor: Uncertainty monotonicity ... KnowledgeOS does not require uncertainty to monotonically decrease. New evidence can increase uncertainty. Initially A appears certain. New evidence reveals A\lor B. The epistemic state becomes more uncertain. Knowledge acquisition need not monotonically reduce uncertain
rationale_evidence.statement: Corrects any assumption of monotonic uncertainty reduction or knowledge growth: new evidence can increase uncertainty, and a committed assertion can later be retracted (A∈K_t, A∉K_{t+1}) — this is epistemic revision, not inconsistency.

rationale_evidence.anchor: Decision consistency ... D_t=f(K_t,\Pi_t). If later K_{t+1} changes, that does not mean D_t was irrational. It means the information state changed. ... Decision invalidation ... if A\in Dependencies(D), then Change(A) should trigger Review(D). KnowledgeChange \rightarrow PotentialDecisionReview.
rationale_evidence.statement: States a later knowledge change does not retroactively make an earlier decision irrational (D_t=f(K_t,Π_t) evaluated at its own time), but a change to a decision's dependency should trigger PotentialDecisionReview.

rationale_evidence.anchor: Complexity ... O(n) versus O(2^n). Our model must eventually track ComplexityClass or at least ComputationalCost. This becomes relevant when KnowledgeOS scales to millions of evidence relationships. ... Graph scalability ... Traceability queries over G=(V,E) may be computationally manageable for loc
rationale_evidence.statement: Notes computational complexity (e.g. O(n) vs O(2^n)) matters at scale, requiring traceability queries have depth limits, scope, relation filters, and time boundaries rather than unrestricted transitive closure.

rationale_evidence.anchor: Conservation of semantics ... summarization may preserve Meaning but not FullEvidence. Therefore a summary cannot replace the original evidence. Summary \rightarrow SourceArtifact through provenance. ... Compression is not lossless ... Information(Summary) < Information(Document). DerivedSummary\neq
rationale_evidence.statement: States DerivedSummary ≠ SourceEvidence (a summary cannot replace the original since Information(Summary)<Information(Document)), requiring transformations declare an InformationLossProfile so KnowledgeOS knows when it must return to the original source.

aliases: Models, Hypotheses, Prediction, Model Selection and Scientific Revision

sources.note: S0909's Step 25Q: the scientific-method layer treating models as first-class, non-destructively-revisable, versioned artifacts distinct from assertions; extends causal-counterfactual-rootcause-algebra (S0908) and mirrors epistemic-revision-error-taxonomy-algebra's (S0905) revision-as-event-addition architecture at the model level.

rows.anchor: Observation\rightarrow Hypothesis\rightarrow Model\rightarrow Prediction\rightarrow Test\rightarrow Revision ... the beginnings of a scientific method for engineering knowledge
rows.statement: Establishes the scientific-method chain Observation->Hypothesis->Model->Prediction->Test->Revision, giving KnowledgeOS 'the beginnings of a scientific method for engineering knowledge'; a causal model is itself a hypothesis, and Model must not silently become Truth.

rows.anchor: O: No outage ... does not automatically prove M_1=False ... PredictionError\neq ModelFalse without further analysis
rows.statement: Worked example: a prediction failure (predicted increased outage probability, observed no outage) does not automatically falsify the model — six alternative explanations listed (wrong model, probabilistic prediction, insufficient sample, absent assumed condition, intervening variable, measurement error) — PredictionError ≠ ModelFalse without further analysis.

rows.anchor: Candidate\rightarrow Proposed\rightarrow Testable\rightarrow Supported\rightarrow Established ... Proposed\rightarrow Refuted ... Supported\rightarrow Weakened ... Established\rightarrow Revised
rows.statement: Defines a five-state model lifecycle (Candidate->Proposed->Testable->Supported->Established) with alternative branches (Proposed->Refuted, Supported->Weakened, Established->Revised).

rows.anchor: Nexus is version 3.70 [assertion] versus Upgrading Nexus reduces security exposure [model] ... Assertion\neq Model
rows.statement: Distinguishes an assertion (a single proposition) from a model (relationships between variables) — Assertion ≠ Model.

rows.anchor: M=(Variables,Relations,Assumptions,Parameters,Scope,Predictions,Version) ... IdentificationStrategy for statistical/causal models
rows.statement: Defines a seven-field Model tuple M=(Variables,Relations,Assumptions,Parameters,Scope,Predictions,Version), with IdentificationStrategy as an optional additional field for statistical/causal models.

rows.anchor: M assumes C=True ... prediction is actually A\land C\rightarrow B ... if C=False, failure of the prediction does not necessarily refute the model ... ModelAssumptions must be explicit
rows.statement: States ModelAssumptions must be explicit and first-class: an unstated assumption C=True means a model's real prediction is A∧C->B, so C being false can explain a prediction failure without refuting the model itself.

rows.anchor: Increasing server capacity reduces response time ... application is CPU-bound; database is not the bottleneck ... If the database is actually the bottleneck ... The model did not necessarily fail. Its applicability conditions were violated
rows.statement: Worked example: a capacity-scaling model's failure when the real bottleneck is the database (violating a CPU-bound assumption) reflects violated applicability conditions, not necessarily model failure.

rows.anchor: Predict(M,X)\rightarrow Y ... P(Y\mid X,M) for probabilistic ... Y=f_M(X) for deterministic ... must record ModelVersion
rows.statement: Formalizes Predict(M,X)->Y for both probabilistic (P(Y|X,M)) and deterministic (Y=f_M(X)) models, requiring recorded ModelVersion.

rows.anchor: Prediction=(Model,Input,Time,ExpectedOutcome,Uncertainty,Assumptions) ... auditable prediction ... Prediction P17 ... Model: NexusUpgradeRisk v2
rows.statement: Defines Prediction as a first-class six-field object (Model,Input,Time,ExpectedOutcome,Uncertainty,Assumptions), worked with a full auditable example record (Prediction P17).

rows.anchor: e=y-\hat y ... Brier score BS=(p-y)^2 ... whether a probabilistic model is calibrated
rows.statement: Defines prediction-error measures across prediction types: numeric residual, classification indicator, and the Brier score for probabilistic predictions, enabling calibration evaluation.

rows.anchor: P(Event)=0.8 ... if approximately 80% of those cases actually produce the event, the model is well calibrated ... Calibration\neq Accuracy ... matters for Sarathi
rows.statement: Defines calibration (repeated 0.8 predictions should be right ~80% of the time) as distinct from accuracy, flagged as mattering for Sarathi's decisions.

rows.anchor: model_quality=0.91 without defining what that means ... ModelAssessment=(PredictiveAccuracy,Calibration,Robustness,Applicability,Complexity,Stability)
rows.statement: Rejects a bare scalar model_quality, requiring a six-dimension ModelAssessment (PredictiveAccuracy,Calibration,Robustness,Applicability,Complexity,Stability), noting different domains emphasize different dimensions.

rows.anchor: TrainingError\approx0 but PredictionError_{new}\gg0 ... overfitting ... HistoricalFit from PredictiveValidity
rows.statement: Defines overfitting (near-zero training error but large new-data prediction error), requiring KnowledgeOS to distinguish HistoricalFit from PredictiveValidity.

rows.anchor: M_1 with 3 parameters, M_2 with 300 ... should not automatically prefer M_2 ... cross-validation; information criteria; regularization; Bayesian model comparison; domain constraints
rows.statement: Rejects automatically preferring a more complex model that equally fits historical data, listing five model-selection principles (cross-validation, information criteria, regularization, Bayesian model comparison, domain constraints).

rows.anchor: AIC=2k-2\ln L, BIC=k\ln n-2\ln L ... a lower AIC/BIC does not mean Model=True ... ModelScore\neq Truth
rows.statement: Gives AIC/BIC formulas as relative comparison criteria, explicitly warning a lower score does not mean Model=True — ModelScore ≠ Truth.

rows.anchor: M_1: Upgrade->Outage and M_2: FirewallChange->Outage ... KnowledgeOS should preserve both {M_1,M_2} ... should not delete M_1 merely because M_2 currently has stronger support
rows.statement: Worked example of two competing causal models both explaining observations, requiring KnowledgeOS to preserve both rather than deleting the currently-weaker one.

rows.anchor: Compare(M_1,M_2,D,C)\rightarrow Assessment ... M_1 preferred / M_2 preferred / Indistinguishable ... extremely important
rows.statement: Defines Compare(M1,M2,D,C)->Assessment with three possible outcomes including the important third case, Indistinguishable.

rows.anchor: M_1\Rightarrow O and M_2\Rightarrow O ... cannot legitimately conclude which is correct ... EvidenceInsufficientForModelSelection ... another form of Zero
rows.statement: Defines underdetermination: when both competing models explain all available observations, EvidenceInsufficientForModelSelection should become another form of Zero.

rows.anchor: M_1\rightarrow M_1' ... ModelRevision=NewModelEvent, not deletion ... mirrors our epistemic revision architecture from 25M
rows.statement: States model revision, like knowledge revision, is a NewModelEvent, never deletion of the prior model — explicitly mirroring the 25M revision architecture.

lineage_claims.quote: This mirrors our epistemic revision architecture from 25M.

rows.anchor: M_1\rightarrow M_2\rightarrow M_3 ... predecessor; changed assumptions; changed parameters; changed structure; reason for revision; supporting evidence ... excellent provenance
rows.statement: Defines model lineage M1->M2->M3, each version recording predecessor, changed assumptions/parameters/structure, revision reason, and supporting evidence, worked with a firewall-then-workload-interaction example.

rows.anchor: P(O\mid M)\approx0 ... strong evidence against M ... P(O\mid M)=0.4 ... much less damaging ... ModelRefutation requires model likelihood, not merely prediction failure
rows.statement: States model falsification strength depends on the model's own predicted likelihood of the observation P(O|M) — a low-likelihood surprise is strong evidence against the model, a merely-unlikely-but-plausible outcome is not — 'ModelRefutation requires model likelihood, not merely prediction failure.'

rows.anchor: P(M_i\mid D)\propto P(D\mid M_i)P(M_i) ... priors must be explicit. KnowledgeOS must not secretly invent them
rows.statement: Defines Bayesian model comparison P(Mi|D) ∝ P(D|Mi)P(Mi), warning priors must be explicit and never secretly invented.

rows.anchor: P(M_1\mid D)=0.55 and P(M_2\mid D)=0.45 ... M1 is the correct model would be unjustified ... ModelsCompeting. Much more honest
rows.statement: Worked example: nearly-equal posterior model probabilities (0.55 vs 0.45) should be reported as ModelsCompeting, not a declared winner — 'much more honest.'

rows.anchor: P(Y\mid D)=\sum_i P(Y\mid M_i,D)P(M_i\mid D) ... model averaging ... requires an explicit probabilistic framework
rows.statement: Defines ensemble/model-averaging P(Y|D)=sum_i P(Y|Mi,D)P(Mi|D) as useful under genuine model uncertainty, but requiring an explicit probabilistic framework.

rows.anchor: ModelRegistry ... Model, ModelVersion, Assumption, Prediction, PredictionResult, ModelAssessment, ModelComparison, ModelRevision ... generic KnowledgeOS layer provides provenance and epistemic infrastructure. The domain context owns the semantics of the models
rows.statement: Proposes a dedicated ModelRegistry bounded-context concept containing eight domain object types, with generic KnowledgeOS supplying provenance/epistemic infrastructure while the domain owns model semantics.

rows.anchor: MC=(InputSchema,OutputSchema,Assumptions,ValidityDomain,Version,EvaluationMethod) ... analogous to an API contract ... without this, a model cannot be safely reused
rows.statement: Defines a six-field ModelContract (InputSchema,OutputSchema,Assumptions,ValidityDomain,Version,EvaluationMethod), analogous to an API contract, required for safe model reuse.

rows.anchor: SecurityRiskModel ... variables meaningless to HotelRevenueModel ... both can exist inside KnowledgeOS without forcing them into one universal semantic model
rows.statement: Reinforces bounded-context-relative model meaning: a security risk model and a hotel revenue model can coexist without a forced universal semantic model.

rows.anchor: ModelOutputContract ... Security BC RiskScore -> Architecture BC SecurityRiskAssessment ... the mapping itself must be documented and versioned
rows.statement: Requires an explicit, documented, versioned ModelOutputContract for cross-bounded-context model-result exchange, worked with a Security->Architecture RiskScore mapping example.

rows.anchor: PredictionCreated, PredictionPublished, PredictionObserved, PredictionEvaluated, PredictionScored, ModelAssessmentUpdated ... produces a feedback loop
rows.statement: Defines a six-stage prediction lifecycle producing a feedback loop into model assessment.

rows.anchor: MODEL->PREDICTION->WORLD->OBSERVATION->COMPARISON->MODEL ASSESSMENT->MODEL REVISION->MODEL ... the scientific-learning loop
rows.statement: Presents the scientific-learning loop diagram consolidating the prediction lifecycle into a closed cycle back to the model.

rows.anchor: KnowledgeOS can therefore learn without training an AI ... ModelRevision based on accumulated evidence ... not necessarily LLM Retraining ... a much broader concept of learning
rows.statement: Argues KnowledgeOS 'learning' need not mean LLM retraining — it can mean model revision based on accumulated evidence, improved rules, better evidence, corrected ontology, better causal models, or calibrated predictions — 'a much broader concept of learning.'

rows.anchor: Zero=MissingVariable ... Lord can ask for Observation(NewVariable) ... ModelFailure\rightarrow KnowledgeGap\rightarrow EvidenceAcquisition
rows.statement: Worked example connecting model failure to the Zero/Lord loop: a repeatedly-failing model missing an important variable produces Zero=MissingVariable, letting Lord request the missing observation — 'an elegant connection between scientific reasoning and the Zero/Lord/Sarathi loop.'

rows.anchor: ModelFailureType=\{ParameterError,DataError,AssumptionViolation,StructuralError,MeasurementError,DistributionShift,UnknownCause\} ... much more useful than model_failed=true
rows.statement: Defines a seven-value ModelFailureType taxonomy, contrasted as much more useful than a bare boolean model_failed flag.

rows.anchor: D_{old}\neq D_{new} ... prediction quality can deteriorate ... DistributionShift ... M(t_1) may not accurately describe W(t_2) ... ModelValidityInterval ... ExpiredModel\neq FalseModel
rows.statement: Defines DistributionShift (deployment distribution diverging from training/validation distribution degrading prediction quality) and temporal model drift, requiring a ModelValidityInterval, and restating ExpiredModel ≠ FalseModel — a model may simply no longer be applicable.

rows.anchor: ModelApproval ... a model can be mathematically valid but unauthorized for production use ... TechnicalValidity\neq GovernanceApproval ... exactly the same principle we established earlier
rows.statement: Restates GovernanceTruth-vs-technical-truth for models: ModelApproval is a governance fact separate from mathematical validity — TechnicalValidity ≠ GovernanceApproval — 'exactly the same principle we established earlier.'

rows.anchor: PredictionID\rightarrow ModelVersion\rightarrow InputEvidence ... PredictionResult\rightarrow Observation ... allows retrospective evaluation
rows.statement: Requires a full model/prediction provenance chain (PredictionID->ModelVersion->InputEvidence, PredictionResult->Observation) enabling retrospective evaluation.

rows.anchor: Prediction=f(ModelVersion,InputSnapshot,Parameters) ... if f is deterministic, replay should reproduce the result ... RandomSeed ... when appropriate
rows.statement: States prediction reproducibility Prediction=f(ModelVersion,InputSnapshot,Parameters), requiring RandomSeed (or equivalent) recording for stochastic models to support replay.

rows.anchor: Test A model versus assertion PASS. Test B prediction failure should not automatically refute a probabilistic model PASS. Test C assumption violation classify AssumptionViolation not ModelFalse PASS. Test D competing models -> Undetermined PASS. Test E model revision does not erase old model PASS. T
rows.statement: Runs seven falsification tests (A-G, all PASS) against the model/prediction/revision machinery: Model!=Assertion holds; a single failed probabilistic prediction should not automatically refute the model; a violated assumption classifies as AssumptionViolation, not ModelFalse; evidence-indistinguishable competing models yield ModelSelection=Undetermined; model revision does not erase the old model; identical ModelVersion+InputSnapshot reproduces the same deterministic prediction; and model drift invalidates applicability without proving universal model falsity.

experiment.hypothesis: The model/prediction/revision machinery (Model!=Assertion, non-destructive revision, reproducibility, drift handling) behaves correctly across seven representative scenarios.
experiment.setup: Seven scenarios A-G spanning model-vs-assertion typing, prediction failure, assumption violation, model competition, model revision, reproducibility, and model drift.
experiment.method: apply the model lifecycle/revision/reproducibility rules to each scenario
experiment.result: All seven scenarios produce the theoretically expected outcome
experiment.interpretation: Confirms the scientific-method layer avoids conflating model failure, assumption violation, and drift.

rows.anchor: H\rightarrow M\rightarrow P\rightarrow O\rightarrow E\rightarrow Assessment(M)\rightarrow Revision(M) ... a complete scientific inference chain
rows.statement: Presents the complete scientific inference chain hypothesis->model->prediction->observation->evidence->model-assessment->model-revision.

rows.anchor: 25Q — PASS ... KnowledgeOS can represent models as first-class, versioned epistemic artifacts whose predictions can be compared with observations and whose validity can be revised without destroying historical model states ... a major step toward a genuine self-correcting knowledge system
rows.statement: Step 25Q self-verdict: PASS — models are first-class, versioned epistemic artifacts, comparable against observations and revisable without destroying historical model states — 'a major step toward a genuine self-correcting knowledge system.'

rows.anchor: P(Outage)=5%. Is that acceptable? ... we cannot answer without knowing Cost(Outage) ... Probability alone does not determine rational action ... Step 25R ... VOI(E)=ExpectedUtility(with E)-ExpectedUtility(now)
rows.statement: Closes by posing the next problem — probability alone cannot determine whether a risk is acceptable without knowing cost/utility ('probability alone does not determine rational action') — transitioning to Step 25R (Decision Theory, Utility, Risk, Value of Information), introducing VOI(E)=ExpectedUtility(with E)-ExpectedUtility(now) as potentially explaining why Zero->Lord->Sarathi is 'a principled decision-making system,' not merely an AI workflow.

lineage_claims.quote: Step 25R — Decision Theory, Utility, Risk, Value of Information and Rational Action

rows.anchor: Model updating from prediction error; calibration update; calibration != causal validity
rows.statement: Given predictions Y-hat_t and actual outcomes Y_t, prediction error e_t=Y_t - Y-hat_t; repeated structured errors may trigger ModelReview. If predicted probabilities are systematically too high (P_pred > P_observed) the model is overconfident and Calibration should be updated -- but calibration does not prove causal correctness, so Calibration != CausalValidity, explicitly said to 'preserve Step 43'.

lineage_claims.quote: This preserves Step 43.

rows.anchor: Continual learning and catastrophic forgetting; immutable evidence, mutable interpretation
rows.statement: A continually learning system M_{t+1}=Learn(M_t,E_{t+1}) risks CatastrophicForgetting (new learning erasing previously valid knowledge); KnowledgeOS should distinguish ModelLearning from KnowledgeHistory, keeping historical knowledge outside the mutable model. States the strong architectural principle: evidence should be immutable, interpretations may evolve -- Evidence_E does not change but Interpretation_t(E) can, modeled as C_1=Interpret(E,M_1), later C_2=Interpret(E,M_2), both historically traceable; this prevents 'the model changed, therefore the historical evidence changed'.
invariants: Evidence is immutable; only its interpretation may evolve

aliases: Step 25C.3: Evidence Dependence and Information Value

sources.note: S0895's Step 25C.3: formalizes InformationGain via Shannon entropy reduction and ValueOfInformation via a decision-theoretic expected-utility formula, runs six falsification tests, distinguishes Epistemic actions (K_t->K_{t+1}) from Operational actions (W_t->W_{t+1}), refines Zero into EpistemicZero vs OperationalZero with a worked migration example, and separates three metrics (Information Gain, Knowledge Gap Reduction, Decision Value) that must never be collapsed into one number; hands off to Step 25D Formal Zero Algebra.

rows.anchor: This is the right next step because we now need to connect evidence aggregation with the question: When is acquiring another piece of evidence actually useful? This is the mathematical bridge between Evidence -> Zero -> Lord.
rows.statement: Frames Step 25C.3's purpose as the mathematical bridge Evidence→Zero→Lord: when is acquiring more evidence actually useful.

rows.anchor: Suppose KnowledgeOS currently has K_t and is considering an investigation action a ... The action may produce E_a. We need to calculate whether obtaining E_a is worthwhile. The first quantity is InformationGain(E_a|K_t) and eventually ValueOfInformation(a|K_t,G).
rows.statement: Defines the two central quantities to be formalized: InformationGain(E_a|K_t) and ValueOfInformation(a|K_t,G) for an investigation action a.

rows.anchor: Suppose KnowledgeOS already knows E_1: NexusVersion=3.69. Now Lord proposes: Read the exact same inventory file again. The resulting evidence is E_2=E_1. The new information should be IG(E_2|E_1)=0. This is a very desirable property. It means KnowledgeOS can recognize: 'I am about to spend resources
rows.statement: First experiment: duplicate-information retrieval must give IG(E2|E1)=0, letting KnowledgeOS recognize it is about to spend resources re-learning something already known.

rows.anchor: For a hypothesis H, Shannon information is I(H)=-log P(H) ... IG(E;H)=Ent(H)-Ent(H|E) [renaming entropy Ent to avoid clash with hypothesis H].
rows.statement: Adopts Shannon entropy-reduction as the formal InformationGain measure: IG(E;H)=Ent(H)-Ent(H|E), renaming entropy notation to avoid clashing with the hypothesis symbol H.

rows.anchor: Suppose P(H)=0.5. The uncertainty is Ent(H)=1 bit. Now an observation gives P(H|E)=0.9. The posterior entropy is lower. Therefore IG(E;H)>0. The observation has reduced uncertainty.
rows.statement: Worked numerical example confirming IG(E;H)>0 when a posterior of 0.9 reduces entropy from the 1-bit prior.

rows.anchor: Suppose E_2=f(E_1). Then even though E_2 is technically another artifact: IG(E_2;H|E_1)=0 or approximately zero. Therefore the more useful quantity is IG(E_2;H|K_t). This asks: How much does this new evidence tell us that we do not already know?
rows.statement: Shows a derived-copy artifact E2=f(E1) gives IG≈0 conditional on E1, motivating the conditional quantity IG(E2;H|K_t) as what KnowledgeOS actually needs (novel information relative to current knowledge, not raw artifact count).

rows.anchor: Suppose E_1 is one restore test. A second independently executed restore test E_2 can provide IG(E_2;H|E_1)>0. This is the mathematical explanation for why independent corroboration can be valuable.
rows.statement: Shows independent corroborating evidence yields IG(E2;H|E1)>0 — the formal information-theoretic explanation for why independent corroboration is valuable.

rows.anchor: If E_2=f(E_1) then IG(E_2;H|E_1)≈0. This gives us a rigorous interpretation of the earlier qualitative rule: Don't count copied evidence twice. It isn't merely a governance convention. It has an information-theoretic interpretation.
rows.statement: Establishes that the earlier 'don't count copied evidence twice' rule has a rigorous information-theoretic interpretation (IG≈0 for derived copies), not merely a governance convention.

rows.anchor: The interesting case is 0 < IG(E_2;H|E_1) < IG(E_2;H). This means E_2 contains some new information, but part of its information was already contained in E_1. This is likely to be extremely common in KnowledgeOS. Vendor documentation -> Internal architecture document -> Human report -> LLM summary.
rows.statement: Identifies partially-dependent evidence (0<IG(E2;H|E1)<IG(E2;H)) as the common case in practice, illustrated by a documentation-lineage chain (vendor doc→architecture doc→human report→LLM summary), none of which can be treated as fully independent.

rows.anchor: Define NovelInformation(E|K) as the information not already represented by the current knowledge state. Conceptually NovelInformation ≈ IG(E;Target|K). This should become one of the quantities available to Lord.
rows.statement: Defines NovelInformation(E|K) ≈ IG(E;Target|K) as a candidate quantity to be made available to Lord.

rows.anchor: Suppose Lord can run Action A: a five-second database query, expected information gain 0.1 bit. Action B: a two-week migration test, expected information gain 1.0 bit. Simply maximizing information would select B. That would be absurd. Therefore InformationGain != Value.
rows.statement: Counterexample showing naive information-maximization would irrationally select a costly two-week test over a cheap query merely for higher bit-count, establishing InformationGain≠Value.

rows.anchor: We need something like ValueOfInformation = ExpectedBenefitFromInformation - Cost. But there is another important term: Risk. Therefore a preliminary formulation is VOI(a) = ExpectedDecisionValueAfter(a) - CurrentDecisionValue - Cost(a) - Risk(a).
rows.statement: Formalizes a preliminary Value-of-Information equation VOI(a)=ExpectedDecisionValueAfter(a)-CurrentDecisionValue-Cost(a)-Risk(a).

rows.anchor: Current best decision a* = argmax_{a in A} EU(a|K_t). Now consider information-gathering action q. After receiving evidence E_q: a*(E_q) = argmax_a EU(a|K_t,E_q). Then VOI(q) = E_{E_q}[max_a EU(a|K_t,E_q)] - max_a EU(a|K_t) - Cost(q). This is a much more rigorous definition.
rows.statement: Gives the rigorous decision-theoretic Value-of-Information formula VOI(q)=E_{E_q}[max_a EU(a|K_t,E_q)]-max_a EU(a|K_t)-Cost(q), the standard expected-utility VOI definition applied to Lord's action selection.

rows.anchor: Lord can now distinguish: Question A: Can I learn something? from Question B: Is learning it worth doing? The first is information theory. The second is decision theory. Thus Lord = InformationAcquisition + DecisionValue.
rows.statement: Distinguishes 'can I learn something' (information theory) from 'is learning it worth doing' (decision theory), decomposing Lord = InformationAcquisition + DecisionValue.

rows.anchor: Suppose our goal is G: Determine whether Nexus rollback is safe. Lord considers: Search the company's office seating plan. It may contain enormous information. But IG(E;G)≈0. Therefore VOI≈0. Lord should reject the action. InformationQuantity != GoalRelevantInformation.
rows.statement: Falsification test: irrelevant-but-information-rich evidence (office seating plan) has IG(E;G)≈0 against the actual goal, so VOI≈0 and Lord correctly rejects it — InformationQuantity≠GoalRelevantInformation.

rows.anchor: Now consider: Execute a restore test against the actual backup. Expected information gain about H: RollbackSafe=True is potentially very high. Therefore IG(E;H|K_t) >> 0. And if the result can change the migration decision: VOI(q) >> 0. This is exactly the type of action Lord should prioritize.
rows.statement: Falsification test: a directly goal-relevant restore test yields IG>>0 and VOI(q)>>0, correctly prioritized by Lord.

rows.anchor: Suppose the migration has already been formally prohibited by governance. Even if we could learn whether Rollback=True the answer cannot change the current authorized decision. Then VOI(q)≈0. ... The same evidence can have HighInformationValue in one context and ZeroDecisionValue in another. Therefo
rows.statement: Falsification test: information that cannot alter an already-governance-prohibited decision has VOI≈0 regardless of its Shannon information content, establishing VOI is goal- and decision-context dependent.

rows.anchor: Suppose migration must happen tomorrow. A test requiring three weeks has potentially useful information. But operationally VOI_effective≈0 if the result arrives after the decision deadline. Therefore time is part of the value calculation.
rows.statement: Falsification test: information arriving after the decision deadline has VOI_effective≈0, establishing time-to-delivery as part of the value calculation.

rows.anchor: Suppose a test could reveal valuable information but requires risking production availability. Then InformationGain>0 but Risk>>0. Therefore Lord should potentially reject it. This gives SafeInformationAcquisition as a governance constraint.
rows.statement: Falsification test: high-information but high-risk acquisition should potentially be rejected, giving SafeInformationAcquisition as a governance constraint on Lord.

rows.anchor: Suppose Lord can ask an infrastructure expert: Is port 8081 reachable from the target network? The answer could be highly informative. But HumanAnswer is itself evidence. Therefore Question -> HumanResponse -> Evidence -> Assessment. The human answer must not bypass the evidence model.
rows.statement: States that a human answer to an information-gathering question is itself Evidence and must flow through Question→HumanResponse→Evidence→Assessment, never bypassing the evidence model.

rows.anchor: Similarly LLM(Document) -> CandidateExtraction. If the document is already known: IG(LLMOutput|Document) may be mostly interpretational, not new factual information. That distinction matters. An LLM can increase SemanticAccessibility without increasing WorldKnowledge. This is a very important distin
rows.statement: Distinguishes an LLM increasing SemanticAccessibility (interpretation) from increasing WorldKnowledge (new factual information) — LLM summarization of an already-known document is mostly interpretational.

rows.anchor: Suppose the document contains 100 pages of architecture information. The LLM summarizes it. KnowledgeOS may gain InterpretationGain>0. But WorldEvidenceGain=0 because the underlying facts were already present. Thus AI can transform knowledge without necessarily adding new evidence. This fits perfect
rows.statement: States AI can transform knowledge (InterpretationGain>0) without adding new evidence (WorldEvidenceGain=0), consistent with the earlier AI-boundary governance principle.

rows.anchor: An AI action can produce: Evidence acquisition (World->Observation); Evidence transformation (Artifact->StructuredEvidence); Semantic interpretation (Evidence->CandidateMeaning); Hypothesis generation (Knowledge->CandidateHypothesis). These have different epistemic values.
rows.statement: Classifies four distinct AI-action epistemic categories (evidence acquisition, evidence transformation, semantic interpretation, hypothesis generation), each with different epistemic value.

rows.anchor: Lord should not simply ask: What should the AI do next? It should choose among InformationActions and OperationalActions. An information action changes K. An operational action changes World. This distinction is becoming mathematically very clean. ... Epistemic action q: K_t -> K_{t+1} through new e
rows.statement: Formalizes two action operators: epistemic action q:K_t→K_{t+1} (changes knowledge) versus operational action a:W_t→W_{t+1} (changes reality) — a clean, mathematically distinct action taxonomy for Lord.

rows.anchor: Therefore the system resembles a partially observable decision process: W_t -> Observation -> K_t -> Action -> W_{t+1}. This is a significant mathematical connection. But we should not yet declare KnowledgeOS to be a POMDP. That framework may be useful for some decision contexts, but KnowledgeOS is
rows.statement: Notes the resulting loop resembles a partially observable decision process (POMDP-like: W_t→Observation→K_t→Action→W_{t+1}), while explicitly warning against prematurely declaring KnowledgeOS to be a POMDP, since KnowledgeOS is broader than that framework.

rows.anchor: Previously Zero(K,I) was a discrepancy. Now we can distinguish EpistemicZero from OperationalZero. Operational zero: Difference between CurrentWorldState and TargetWorldState. Epistemic zero: Difference between CurrentKnowledge and KnowledgeRequiredByContract. This is a major refinement.
rows.statement: Refines Zero(K,I) into two distinct kinds: OperationalZero (CurrentWorldState vs TargetWorldState gap) and EpistemicZero (CurrentKnowledge vs KnowledgeRequiredByContract gap) — a major refinement of the Zero concept.

rows.anchor: Target: Migration can be safely executed. Current world: Nexus 3.69, Backup exists, Target environment exists. Operationally perhaps only MigrationScriptMissing. But epistemically: Rollback effectiveness = unknown, Firewall = conflicted, Capacity = unknown, Governance approval = missing. Therefore Z
rows.statement: Worked migration example showing Zero_epistemic (four unresolved epistemic gaps) can be much larger than Zero_operational (one missing script) — declared one of the central ideas of KnowledgeOS.

rows.anchor: Lord(q) ≈ argmax_q ExpectedReductionInDecisionCriticalGap(q) / (Cost(q)+Risk(q)). This is still provisional, but it is an excellent candidate.
rows.statement: Proposes Lord's provisional real optimization objective: maximize ExpectedReductionInDecisionCriticalGap(q)/(Cost(q)+Risk(q)) over candidate epistemic actions q, explicitly marked provisional.

rows.anchor: Our emerging language now includes: Evidence; Information Gain; Knowledge Gap; Decision-Critical Gap; Epistemic Action; Operational Action; Value of Information. These are not merely technical terms. They represent distinct domain concepts.
rows.statement: Consolidates seven emerging ubiquitous-language domain concepts (Evidence, Information Gain, Knowledge Gap, Decision-Critical Gap, Epistemic Action, Operational Action, Value of Information) as genuine DDD domain terms, not merely technical jargon.

rows.anchor: Now attack our proposed model. Test 1 Duplicate evidence: IG=0. Good. Test 2 Independent evidence: IG>0. Good. Test 3 Irrelevant evidence: IG_goal≈0. Good. Test 4 Information arrives after decision deadline: VOI≈0. Good. Test 5 Information cannot alter authorized decision: VOI≈0. Good. Test 6 High i
rows.statement: Runs six falsification tests against the IG/VOI model (duplicate, independent, irrelevant, deadline-expired, decision-incapable, dangerous-acquisition), all passing, concluding the model behaves sensibly.

experiment.design: Six adversarial probe cases against the IG/VOI formalization

rows.anchor: Suppose an action produces an unexpected result. Lord predicts P(E_1)=0.8 and P(E_2)=0.2. Reality produces E_2. The value of the information cannot be calculated correctly unless the predictive model itself is reasonably calibrated. Therefore VOI depends on the quality of the predictive model. We ca
rows.statement: Identifies that VOI calculation depends on the predictive model being well-calibrated (illustrated by a low-probability outcome actually occurring), an assumption that cannot be hidden.

rows.anchor: The formula VOI=ExpectedBenefit-Cost-Risk looks simple. But what is Benefit? For one organization 1 hour might be worth €100. For a safety-critical system, preventing one failure might be worth millions. Therefore UtilityModel must be domain-specific. This should belong to the Decision Context, not
rows.statement: Flags Benefit/UtilityModel as inherently domain-specific (worked hourly-cost vs safety-critical-failure example) and assigns it to the Decision Context, not the epistemic kernel.

rows.anchor: We have been using InformationGain in the Shannon/statistical sense. But KnowledgeOS may also need KnowledgeGain which is not necessarily measured in bits. For example: Discovering that a mandatory governance approval is missing could be enormously important even though it doesn't naturally map to a
rows.statement: Establishes InformationGain≠KnowledgeGain≠DecisionValue: a missing-mandatory-governance-approval discovery is enormously important epistemically/decisionally despite mapping poorly to Shannon entropy reduction.

rows.anchor: I now recommend explicitly separating: Information Gain (IG) — how much uncertainty is mathematically reduced. Knowledge Gap Reduction (KGR) — how much of the epistemic contract has been satisfied. Decision Value (DV) — how much the new information can improve the decision. These are related but not
rows.statement: Defines three explicitly separated metrics: Information Gain (IG, entropy reduction), Knowledge Gap Reduction (KGR, epistemic-contract satisfaction), and Decision Value (DV, decision-improvement potential).

rows.anchor: Suppose a document clarifies an obscure architecture detail. It provides IG>0. But it is irrelevant to the current migration contract: KGR≈0. And cannot alter the decision: DV=0. Conversely, discovering GovernanceApprovalMissing may have little conventional Shannon-information interpretation but KGR
rows.statement: Worked contrasting example (obscure architecture detail: IG>0,KGR≈0,DV=0 vs GovernanceApprovalMissing: low IG, KGR>>0, DV>>0) arguing KnowledgeOS cannot be reduced to information theory alone.

rows.anchor: We have now established a useful three-level structure: Evidence -> Information -> KnowledgeGap -> DecisionValue with different mathematical semantics at each layer. And therefore Lord should optimize decision-relevant knowledge acquisition, not raw information acquisition.
rows.statement: Consolidates the three-level structure Evidence→Information→KnowledgeGap→DecisionValue (distinct semantics per layer) into the governing principle that Lord should optimize decision-relevant knowledge acquisition, not raw information acquisition.

rows.anchor: 25C.3 -- PASS, with a new refinement. We can formally connect EvidenceDependency to ConditionalInformationGain and then to ValueOfInformation. But we must not collapse IG, KGR, VOI into one universal number.
rows.statement: Verdicts Step 25C.3 PASS-with-refinement: EvidenceDependency formally connects to ConditionalInformationGain and then ValueOfInformation, but IG/KGR/VOI must never be collapsed into a single universal number.

rows.anchor: We can now write a considerably stronger chain: Input -> Evidence -> EvidenceGraph -> Assessment -> Inference -> KnowledgeState; then KnowledgeState -> EpistemicZero -> KnowledgeGap; then KnowledgeGap -> InformationAction -> Evidence; or KnowledgeState -> DecisionInference -> Recommendation -> Opera
rows.statement: Consolidates the current full KnowledgeOS mathematical chain spanning evidence intake, epistemic-gap computation, information-seeking feedback loop, and the decision→action→world-change→observation loop.

rows.anchor: There is one question we now cannot avoid: How exactly should Zero calculate the difference between the current knowledge state and the knowledge required by the goal? We have used Zero conceptually many times, but we have not yet given it a rigorous mathematical definition. So I recommend the next
rows.statement: Proposes Step 25D (Formal Zero Algebra) to rigorously define Zero(K,G,EC), listing ten states it must distinguish (known/unknown/insufficient/conflicting/stale/invalid/prohibited/irrelevant/satisfied/partially-satisfied) and posing whether Zero can be computed from KnowledgeState rather than being an AI-generated narrative.

formal.anchor: Suppose KnowledgeOS currently has K_t and is considering an investigation action a ... The action may produce E_a. We need to calculate whether obtaining E_a is worthwhile. The first quantity is InformationGain(E_a|K_t) and eventually ValueOfInformation(a|K_t,G).

aliases: Step 11: Uncertainty Propagation and Derived Knowledge

sources.note: S0865's Step 11: six uncertainty origins, a multidimensional uncertainty vector and derivation dependency graph, method-dependent propagation, marginal-vs-joint-confidence counterexample, provenance-universal vs numerical-propagation-calculus-dependent split, inference sufficiency and missing-premise gap discovery, cyclic-inference fixpoint/monotonicity requirements, and U1-U10 invariants culminating in a 'universal uncertainty contract, not formula' result; hands off to Step 12 (identity/entity resolution/semantic equivalence).

rows.anchor: A common mistake is to say A_1,A_2\Rightarrow A_3 therefore A_3 has "the same confidence" as A_1,A_2. That is generally false. The epistemic quality of a derived proposition depends on what kind of inference produced it, what premises it depends on, how those premises depend on one another, and what
rows.statement: Warns against assuming a derived proposition inherits its premises' confidence wholesale; its epistemic quality depends on the inference kind, premise dependencies, and the inference rule's own uncertainty.

rows.anchor: The fundamental problem ... A_1=Strong and A_2=Weak. A_3=A_1\land A_2 ... It cannot simply inherit Strong. Nor should we arbitrarily assign Weak. ... \Sigma_{derived} = Propagate_\rho(\Sigma_{premises},Rule,Method,Dependency,Context)
rows.statement: Defines Σ_derived=Propagate_ρ(Σ_premises,Rule,Method,Dependency,Context) as the general propagation function, illustrated by a conjunction of a Strong and a Weak premise where neither naive inheritance is correct.

rows.anchor: First distinction: uncertainty has different origins ... Premise uncertainty U_{premise} ... Inference uncertainty U_{inference} ... Model uncertainty U_{model} ... Measurement uncertainty U_{measurement} ... Semantic uncertainty U_{semantic} ... Context uncertainty U_{context} ... Uncertainty\neq o
rows.statement: Enumerates six distinct uncertainty origins — premise, inference, model, measurement, semantic, context — establishing Uncertainty ≠ one universal quantity.

rows.anchor: This confirms our multidimensional model ... U_A=(U_{source},U_{measurement},U_{semantic},U_{inference},U_{model},U_{context}) ... more rigorous than U_A=0.3. A scalar may later be derived if a policy needs one.
rows.statement: Defines a six-dimension uncertainty vector U_A, more rigorous than a bare scalar U_A=0.3, from which a policy-specific scalar may later be derived.

rows.anchor: Dependency graph ... G_D=(V,E_D) ... A1, A2 → A3 → A5 ... Deps(A_3)=\{A_1,A_2\} and Deps(A_5)=\{A_3\}. Therefore uncertainty can propagate through the graph.
rows.statement: Defines a derivation dependency graph G_D=(V,E_D) with Deps(A) giving direct premise sets, through which uncertainty can propagate.

rows.anchor: But propagation depends on the inference method ... y=2x ... \sigma_y=2\sigma_x=0.2 ... a mathematical propagation rule. But now consider ... x is probably caused by y ... an abductive inference. Its uncertainty cannot be propagated using the same formula. PropagationFunction depends on InferenceMet
rows.statement: Shows via a linear-uncertainty-propagation example (y=2x, σ_y=2σ_x) contrasted with an abductive inference that the propagation function itself depends on the inference method, not a single universal formula.

rows.anchor: Deterministic derivation ... A_1\vdash Q ... the derivation itself does not introduce statistical uncertainty. However, the premises may still have epistemic uncertainty. Deterministic rule \not\Rightarrow uncertain premises. The rule may be certain while its inputs are not.
rows.statement: Distinguishes rule certainty from premise certainty: a deterministic derivation rule does not itself add uncertainty, but its premises may still be epistemically uncertain — Deterministic rule ⇏ uncertain premises.

rows.anchor: Statistical inference ... \hat\theta=10.2 with SE(\hat\theta)=0.4. The uncertainty belongs to the statistical inference. KnowledgeOS must preserve Estimate=10.2 and Uncertainty=0.4 rather than reducing the output to 10.2.
rows.statement: Requires KnowledgeOS to preserve a statistical estimate together with its standard error (e.g. 10.2 ± 0.4) rather than collapsing to the point estimate alone.

rows.anchor: Correlated evidence ... E_2=Copy(E_1), then Information(E_2\mid E_1)\approx0. Dependency structure must participate in uncertainty/support propagation.
rows.statement: Restates that strongly correlated/copied evidence adds near-zero additional information, so dependency structure must participate in uncertainty/support propagation, not be treated as independent.

rows.anchor: Unknown dependency ... a conservative policy might produce Support_{combined}\leq Support_{assuming independence}. But that inequality is policy-dependent, not a universal mathematical theorem. The kernel should preserve Dependency=Unknown. The assessment calculus decides what to do.
rows.statement: Notes a conservative policy may cap combined support below the independence assumption when dependency is unknown, but this inequality is policy-dependent, not a universal theorem — the kernel only preserves Dependency=Unknown.

rows.anchor: The most important statistical distinction ... P(A)=0.9 and P(B)=0.9 ... If independent P(A\land B)=0.81. If perfectly dependent P(A\land B)=0.9. Marginal confidence does not determine joint confidence. This is a major reason KnowledgeOS cannot use naive confidence multiplication.
rows.statement: Uses two 0.9-confidence propositions to show joint confidence ranges from 0.81 (independent) to 0.9 (perfectly dependent) — marginal confidence does not determine joint confidence, ruling out naive confidence multiplication.

rows.anchor: Statistical propagation needs a model ... Y=f(X_1,\ldots,X_n) ... Var(Y)\approx J\Sigma_XJ^T ... Covariance matters. This maps beautifully to our evidence-dependency model.
rows.statement: Notes formal statistical uncertainty propagation Var(Y)≈JΣ_XJ^T requires the full covariance matrix, mapping naturally onto the evidence-dependency model — covariance matters, not just marginal uncertainties.

rows.anchor: KnowledgeOS should therefore preserve dependency, not just scores ... A1 confidence = 0.9, A2 confidence = 0.9 ... instead A1, A2, Dependency(A1,A2) = Independent / Dependent / Unknown. Then a calculus can determine the appropriate combination. This is one of the strongest architectural consequences
rows.statement: Argues KnowledgeOS must store per-pair Dependency status alongside confidence scores rather than bare scores alone, called one of the strongest architectural consequences of the theory.

rows.anchor: Derived knowledge should retain its dependency graph ... A_3=f(A_1,A_2). Basis(A_3)=\{A_1,A_2\}. If A_1 is retracted, we do not automatically retract A_3. Instead Reassess(A_3). This follows directly from Step 9.
rows.statement: Requires derived assertions retain their basis (Basis(A3)={A1,A2}), so retracting one premise triggers Reassess, not automatic retraction — following directly from Step 9's dependency-propagation invariant.

rows.anchor: Support propagation ... S_3=PropagateSupport_\rho(S_1,S_2,R,D,C) ... S_3=\min(S_1,S_2) ... S_3=S_1\times S_2 ... S_3=f(S_1,S_2,D). There is no universal formula.
rows.statement: Defines abstract support propagation S_3=PropagateSupport_ρ(S1,S2,R,D,C), showing min, product, and dependency-adjusted formulas as different rule-specific instances — no universal formula.

rows.anchor: Uncertainty propagation ... U_3=PropagateUncertainty_\rho(U_1,U_2,R,D,C) ... The kernel stores uncertainty semantics; the calculus performs uncertainty propagation.
rows.statement: Defines U_3=PropagateUncertainty_ρ(U1,U2,R,D,C) analogously to support propagation, with the architecture rule that the kernel stores uncertainty semantics while the calculus performs the actual propagation.

rows.anchor: A useful distinction: epistemic versus aleatory uncertainty ... Aleatory uncertainty Intrinsic variability/randomness ... Epistemic uncertainty Uncertainty caused by lack of knowledge ... We don't know which version is deployed. KnowledgeOS primarily deals with epistemic uncertainty, but may also en
rows.statement: Distinguishes aleatory uncertainty (intrinsic randomness, e.g. X~N(μ,σ²)) from epistemic uncertainty (lack of knowledge, e.g. unknown deployed version), noting KnowledgeOS primarily deals with the latter but should not collapse the two when both are relevant.

rows.anchor: Example: infrastructure ... Backup configured ... Restore test succeeded ... Backup is operationally recoverable. A_1,A_2\Rightarrow A_3. But suppose A_2 is missing. Then A_1 alone may support Configured but not OperationallyRecoverable. Missing premise \Rightarrow Derived proposition remains unreso
rows.statement: Worked backup-recoverability example showing that a missing premise (no restore test) leaves the derived proposition unresolved rather than falsely supported.

rows.anchor: This gives us a concept of inference sufficiency ... Complete(R,\Gamma) meaning all required premises are available at the required epistemic level. Complete(R,\Gamma)=False \Rightarrow A_3 cannot be deductively derived. An LLM may still hypothesize A_3, but it must not label it as deterministic der
rows.statement: Defines inference-sufficiency predicate Complete(R,Γ): if false, A3 cannot be deductively derived, though an LLM may hypothesize it as long as it is never mislabeled deterministic derivation.

rows.anchor: Partial derivation ... Candidate(A_3) and MissingPremise(A_2). This directly generates a discrepancy \Delta_{missing premise}. Lord can then search for evidence for A_2. So inference becomes another mechanism for gap discovery. Inference \rightarrow MissingPremise \rightarrow Discrepancy \rightarrow
rows.statement: Shows a missing premise generates a Candidate(A3)+MissingPremise(A2) state that becomes a discrepancy Lord can act on, establishing the feedback loop Inference→MissingPremise→Discrepancy→EvidenceAcquisition — inference as another gap-discovery mechanism, i.e. KnowledgeOS can infer what it needs to know in order to infer what it wants to know.

rows.anchor: Uncertainty propagation through chains ... A_1\rightarrow A_2\rightarrow A_3\rightarrow A_4 ... For a probabilistic model P(A_4\mid A_1) ... For deterministic rules A_1\vdash A_2\vdash A_3\vdash A_4. For defeasible rules, an intermediate conclusion may be defeated later. InferenceDepth can affect ep
rows.statement: Shows chained inference (A1→A2→A3→A4) behaves differently under probabilistic, deterministic, and defeasible rule regimes — inference depth affects reliability, but through no single universal formula.

rows.anchor: LLM chains ... Document → LLM extraction → Assertion A1 → LLM interpretation → Assertion A2 → LLM synthesis → Assertion A3 ... We must preserve the entire chain: D\rightarrow A_1\rightarrow A_2\rightarrow A_3. A3 inherits dependency on the entire chain. This does not mean its uncertainty must be num
rows.statement: Traces an LLM extraction→interpretation→synthesis chain (Document→A1→A2→A3), requiring the full lineage preserved even though numerical uncertainty need not be multiplied along the chain.

rows.anchor: This distinction is essential ... Uncertainty propagation A mathematical transformation of uncertainty. Provenance propagation Preservation of the causal/derivational basis. KnowledgeOS must always do provenance propagation. It may do quantitative uncertainty propagation only when the chosen calculu
rows.statement: Distinguishes universal Provenance propagation (always required) from calculus-dependent Numerical uncertainty propagation (only when the chosen calculus supports it) — called a major theoretical result.

rows.anchor: Derived epistemic state ... \Sigma_D = F_\rho(\Sigma_1,\ldots,\Sigma_n,R,D,C) ... Acquisition=Derived and Method=R.Method. Acquisition = Derived, Method = Deduction, Rule = R-17 ... or Method = StatisticalInference, Model = M-04 ... or Acquisition = Generated, Method = LLMInterpretation.
rows.statement: Defines the derived epistemic state Σ_D=F_ρ(Σ1,...,Σn,R,D,C) requiring an explicit Acquisition=Derived/Generated field and Method (Deduction/Rule, StatisticalInference/Model, LLMInterpretation) recorded per assertion.

rows.anchor: Validity propagation ... Validity(A_2) \subseteq Validity(A_1) may be appropriate. But if another premise has shorter validity, A_2 may be constrained by the intersection Validity(A_2) \subseteq \bigcap_i Validity(A_i). Again, the exact semantics are policy-dependent.
rows.statement: Defines validity propagation for derived assertions: Validity(A2)⊆Validity(A1) in the simple case, or the intersection over all premises when several bound it, with the exact semantics policy-dependent.

rows.anchor: Temporal propagation ... A derived assertion ... should not silently become current in 2026. TemporalValidity must propagate through derivation.
rows.statement: Requires temporal validity to propagate through derivation, so a derived assertion about a 2024-valid premise does not silently become current later.

rows.anchor: Conflict propagation ... A_3=f(A_1) may therefore inherit a dependency on the contested premise. It need not automatically become contested, but KnowledgeOS should know DependsOnContested(A_3,A_1). Propagation of dependency \neq automatic propagation of status.
rows.statement: Distinguishes dependency propagation from status propagation: a derived assertion depending on a contested premise is recorded as DependsOnContested, without automatically inheriting the Contested status itself — that remains a policy decision.

rows.anchor: A formal dependency operator ... D(A) ... transitive dependencies are D^*(A) ... D^*(A) = \bigcup_{x\in D(A)}(\{x\}\cup D^*(x)). This gives us a computable dependency closure for finite acyclic derivation graphs.
rows.statement: Defines the transitive dependency closure D*(A)=∪_{x∈D(A)}({x}∪D*(x)), computable for finite acyclic derivation graphs.

rows.anchor: Cyclic inference ... A_1\rightarrow A_2 and A_2\rightarrow A_1. We have a cycle. KnowledgeOS should not blindly use recursive support amplification. Cycles require explicit fixpoint or cycle policy. ... Fixpoint semantics ... K^*=T(K^*) ... whether a fixpoint exists, is unique, and is computable dep
rows.statement: Warns cyclic inference (A1→A2→A1) must never blindly amplify support, requiring an explicit fixpoint (K*=T(K*)) or cycle policy, with monotonicity (K1⊆K2⇒T(K1)⊆T(K2)) required for well-behaved iterative closure and explicit revision semantics needed when it fails.

rows.anchor: Computational conclusion ... Can uncertainty and derivation be computed? Yes, when: the evidence graph is finite; inference rules are explicit; dependency relationships are represented; the selected calculus is computationally defined; uncertainty semantics are specified. But: There is no universal
rows.statement: Concludes uncertainty/derivation computation is tractable under five conditions (finite graph, explicit rules, represented dependencies, computationally-defined calculus, specified uncertainty semantics), while there is no universal algorithm for arbitrary natural-language inference — Computable kernel operations must be distinguished from AI-assisted semantic interpretation.

rows.anchor: KnowledgeOS computational contract ... Every computationally asserted result must declare its inference method and its derivation basis. Derived(A) \Rightarrow (Method(A),Premises(A),Rule/Model(A),Version(A)). If these are unavailable: Status(A)\neq DeterministicallyDerived.
rows.statement: States the computational contract: every derived assertion must declare Method, Premises, Rule/Model, and Version — absent these, its status can never be DeterministicallyDerived.

rows.anchor: The complete uncertainty model ... A=(P,E,\Sigma,\Omega,D,\Pi,Ctx,\tau) ... \Sigma=(Acquisition,Support,Uncertainty,Validity) ... \Omega=(Acceptance,Commitment,Contest) ... D=DependencyGraph.
rows.statement: Consolidates the assertion model as A=(Proposition,Evidence,Σ,Ω,DependencyGraph,Provenance,Context,Time), integrating the epistemic (Σ) and governance (Ω) states with an explicit dependency graph.

rows.anchor: The most important Step 11 principles ... U1 — Preserve uncertainty ... U2 — Method dependence ... U3 — Dependency dependence ... U4 — Provenance is universal ... U5 — Unknown dependency remains unknown ... U6 — Revision triggers reassessment ... U7 — Missing premises remain gaps ... U8 — Statistica
rows.statement: States ten candidate invariants U1-U10: derived knowledge must not silently become certain; propagation depends on inference method; dependency affects aggregation; provenance is universally retained; unknown≠independent; premise revision triggers dependent reassessment; missing premises remain gaps (unresolved inference); statistical uncertainty is retained; LLM output ≠ deterministic derivation; derived chains must not create independent evidence merely through repetition.

rows.anchor: Step 11 verdict ... THEORETICALLY RESOLVED AT THE FRAMEWORK LEVEL ... KnowledgeOS does not need one universal uncertainty formula. It needs a universal uncertainty contract. Origin + Method + Dependency + Provenance + UncertaintySemantics + Validity. The selected inference/assessment calculus then d
rows.statement: Declares Step 11 theoretically resolved at the framework level with the major result that KnowledgeOS needs a universal uncertainty contract (Origin+Method+Dependency+Provenance+UncertaintySemantics+Validity), not a universal uncertainty formula.

rows.anchor: Where we are after Step 11 ... Input \rightarrow Evidence \rightarrow Relations \rightarrow Assessment \rightarrow Acceptance \rightarrow KnowledgeState \rightarrow Discrepancy \rightarrow CandidateAction \rightarrow NewEvidence \rightarrow Inference \rightarrow DerivedKnowledge \rightarrow Uncertai
rows.statement: Assembles the full pipeline from Input through Evidence/Relations/Assessment/Acceptance/KnowledgeState/Discrepancy/CandidateAction/NewEvidence/Inference/DerivedKnowledge/UncertaintyPropagation to RevisedKnowledgeState, with provenance preserved across the entire chain.

rows.anchor: Step 12 — The next problem ... How does KnowledgeOS know that two propositions actually refer to the same thing, concept, entity, event, or state? ... "Nexus" "Nexus Repository" "Nexus3" "nexus3.dgverlag.de" "the artifact repository" "the old Nexus server" ... Step 12 — Identity, Entity Resolution,
rows.statement: Poses Step 12: identity, entity resolution, and semantic equivalence across differently-named references to the same entity (six example Nexus aliases) and differently-worded but possibly equivalent propositions, called one of the most important remaining computational tests since duplicate/contradiction/dependency/aggregation/update reliability all depend on it.
